It’s the first exhibition in the MFA’s history dedicated solely to a musician and the archive’s only stop.","Kristen Hoskins, director of public programs, co-curated what promises to be a blockbuster show. In an announcement on Tuesday she said the MFA is inviting visitors to take an intimate look at the fashion and instruments of one of today’s most influential cultural figures.","\"I'm excited to welcome audiences across generations to this unique experience at the Museum,” Hoskins said, “especially Swifties, whose passion and community building are an essential part of Taylor's story.\"","\u003cspan data-index=\"1\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","The Eras Tour grossed more than $2 billion in ticket sales. Like the tour, the exhibition spans Swift’s 20-year career, from her self-titled 2006 debut album to 2025’s “The Life of a Showgirl.” Vignettes built around “Tim McGraw” (2006) and “The Fate of Ophelia” (2025) bookend the museum’s exhibition.","Other highlights include Swift’s midnight-blue, crystal-laden Zuhair Murad bodysuit, the Deering banjo from her Broadway-inspired “Speak Now” world tour and the mandolin she played in the 2020 video for “Willow” and the typewriter seen in her 2024 video for “Fortnight.”","\"With over a century of experience celebrating the art of musical instruments and fashion, the MFA is the perfect place to host an exhibition exploring Taylor Swift's exceptional artistry,\" Jared Katz, curator of musical instruments, said in the announcement. \"I'm delighted that we are able to make accessible these instruments and costumes from all of Taylor’s eras, which represent a remarkable musical journey across genres over the last 20 years.”","Katz said he hopes visitors leave with a deeper appreciation for Swift’s creativity and talent, “and maybe even get inspired to start creating music of their own.\"","Timed tickets cost $40 and go on sale to the public at 6 p.m. on Dec. 13, which is Swift’s 37th birthday. organizing for the Massachusetts Union of Public Housing Tenants. \"That's what we are hearing mainly — that people are going to be afraid of actually revealing these documents, and they are going to href=\"https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/12/2026-23003/housing-and-community-development-act-of-1980-verification-of-eligible-status\"\u003erule\u003c/a\u003e, issued last Thursday by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, would require all tenants who live in federally-funded housing to show proof of U.S. citizenship or lawful immigration status. It goes into effect on Dec. 15 and tenants must submit proof of status by March 14.","Since 1995, federal policy has allowed mixed-status families to live together in HUD-assisted housing. The government only provides rental assistance to eligible family members, and families pay a higher, pro-rated share of rent.","The Trump administration's new rule would eliminate that arrangement. Advocates say it would potentially force families to choose between remaining together outside public housing or separating so eligible household members can retain assistance.","\"We believe that a lot of people are going to be displaced,\" Patiño said. \"It's very tragic because it's going to divide families.\"","In a statement \u003ca href=\"https://www.hud.gov/news/hud-no-26-091\"\u003eonline\u003c/a\u003e, Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner has said the agency is implementing the rule because it wants to ensure only citizens and eligible immigrants live in federally-subsidized housing.","It cited the long waiting lists for the housing as a reason to further inspect tenants.","“It’s unacceptable that America’s homeless veterans, disabled, elderly, and victims of domestic violence languish on waitlists while illegals and ineligibles scam our system. American taxpayers will no longer foot the bill. Promises made, promises kept,” Turner said.","The office claims it and the Department of Homeland Security audited the agency and found nearly 200,000 tenants who had incomplete or unknown eligibility verification.","The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan research institute, estimates that nearly \u003ca href=\"https://www.cbpp.org/sites/default/files/12-12-25hous.pdf\"\u003e1,000 households\u003c/a\u003e in Massachusetts would be affected by the change. The center also finds Massachusetts would have the fourth-highest number of affected households, behind California, New York and Texas.","The administration had attempted to implement similar requirements in 2019 and reintroduced the proposal this past February.","A coalition of 22 state attorneys general, including Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell, sent \u003ca href=\"https://oag.maryland.gov/News/Documents/pdfs/Mixed%20Status%20Rule%20Cmt%20Ltr%204.21.pdf\"\u003ea letter\u003c/a\u003e to the housing agency in April opposing the changes.","Patiño also questioned whether the Trump administration has considered the financial and administrative costs of enforcing the new requirements.","The policy could also affect U.S. citizens who live in mixed-status households, particularly those who may have difficulty obtaining or submitting the required documents before recertification deadlines, she said.","The more than \u003ca href=\"https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/assthsg.html\"\u003e180,000\u003c/a\u003e Massachusetts households that receive federal housing assistance would be required to prove their citizenship or lawful immigration status under the rule.","\"So many actually American citizens, they are going to be affected because they are not going to be able to recertificate on time and bring those documents,\" Patiño said.","A spokesperson for Massachusetts’ Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, which oversees state-subsidized public housing and shelter systems, said the agency is aware of the final rule change and assessing any potential impacts in the state.","Beyond the potential displacement of families, Rey Santana, president of the Mystic Tenants Association in Somerville, said the policy could add pressure to Massachusetts' already strained affordable housing and shelter systems.","“How would they get into these programs when they're already so overflown with people who have already been there,” Santana said.","With rising housing costs already a concern for many Massachusetts residents, Santana warned that forcing more people out of public housing could deepen the state's affordable housing challenges.","\"Even if you're not directly affected, you're still affected by this change,\" Santana If built, it would be the among largest data centers in the country.","Because the town currently has no zoning laws related to data centers, Sutton’s planning board is exploring options to add a bylaw for data centers to be built in the town.","Town officials said at the meeting that the campus would bring in nearly $28 million in tax revenue each year, which could lower the tax bill of an average single-family home and help close the town’s growing budget deficit.","But residents in attendance said they are worried about the data center’s impact on the environment, public health and home values.","\u003cspan data-index=\"1\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","Shawn Buzzell, who has lived in Sutton for three years, stood outside the town hall collecting signatures on a petition before the meeting. He said the petition, which had more than 300 signatures as of Monday night, calls for a special town meeting for residents to vote on the petition’s definition of data centers and prohibit their construction in Sutton.","He said he’s against the proposed data center because he’s concerned that it will put residents at risk of higher electricity costs and noise pollution.","“They’re sticking them in the middle of people’s neighborhoods,” Buzzell said. “They wedge these in there and it’s not because it’s the right place to put it, it’s because it’s the cheapest place to put it. They end up ruining a lot of people’s lives, destroying quality of life, destroying household resale value, just so they can make themselves a little bit more extra money, and that’s not fair.”","Crystal Smith, a Sutton resident for 15 years, said she has been \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/npr/nx-s1-5927288/data-center-election-voters-ai\"\u003efollowing the news about data centers\u003c/a\u003e, but never expected one to be built in the “tiny town” of Sutton.","“We don’t have the space for that, we don’t have the resources for that and it would impact way too many things here,” Smith said.","About 75 residents attended Monday night’s planning board meeting. Some held signs that read, “NO DATA CENTERS” and “NO DATA CENTERS IN SUTTON.” Others chimed in during the meeting, voicing their disapproval of the project.","WBUR reached out to The Kraft Group for comment, but did not receive a response in time for publication.","In a memorandum outlining the project, the town said the proposal is tentative. It drew 1.29 million votes against it and nearly 1.26 million in support. Healey has made housing production one of her top priorities and addressed the failure of the initiative petition at the Boston Globe Summit on Tuesday.","\"My job is to make sure that all regions are thriving, and that means housing production across the state. It may look a little different in different parts of the state, but I think, you know, I was disappointed that that question failed,\" Healey said. \"I also think there's a new opportunity. It didn't fail by much, and I think part of it was a lack of public education about what that would actually do in terms of helping us build these starter homes. So, you know, I think I think we can make that happen.\"","Question 7 would have enabled single-family homes to be built on lots as small as 5,000 square feet that have at least 50 feet of land bordering the street and access to public water and sewer services. While supporters argued the question would have created momentum to build starter homes and help seniors downsize, the measure did not explicitly mandate the size of the homes. The Massachusetts Municipal Association opposed the ballot question.","Globe reporter Emma Platoff, who engaged Healey in a Q\u0026amp;A on stage to open the two-day event, asked the governor if she would like to see the Legislature take on the housing policy in Question 7 as its own piece of legislation and pass it.","\"Sure. Yeah, along with a host of other things because there is an urgency about housing and urgency about so many things. So I'd like to see action,\" the governor said.","The Legislature did not tackle a statewide housing-dedicated bill this session, but Democrats tried to take what Sen. Julian Cyr called a \"housing-in-all-policy strategy approach\" that saw drops of housing policy sprinkled into budgets and other policy legislation. (Mark Schiefelbein/AP)\n                        \u003c/figcaption\u003e\n                    \u003c/figure\u003e","MANILA, Philippines — President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.","Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.","The visit marks Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.","As he descended the stairs from Air Force One, Trump pumped his fist. A child handed him small American and Philippine flags, which Trump waved and then swooped in big circular motions as he smiled. The U.S. president was greeted by a marching band playing \"YMCA\" while he walked to a waiting helicopter.","\u003ch3\u003eTrump to be feted at the annual ASEAN summit\u003c/h3\u003e","Trump's first hours in the Philippines will include all the reassuring optics from Washington's oldest treaty ally in Asia, including a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the \"guest of honor\" at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.","The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.","First on Trump's agenda Tuesday is a meeting with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan that have aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific. It will be their first meeting since Trump returned to the White House last year.","Trump is then scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats.","The U.S. had announced a trade framework last October in which Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing U.S. autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. At the time, the Trump administration said Thailand would also spend more than $18 billion on U.S. aircraft and buy U.S. farm goods and liquefied natural gas.","The U.S. Supreme Court overturned in February the 19% tariff that Trump placed on goods from Thailand. The administration sought replacement tariffs in July by levying a 12.5% tax on imports from Thailand for not taking steps to oppose the use of forced labor.","Before the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump will participate in what's billed as a \"special summit\" with the ASEAN leaders, where they are expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region's longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.","Washington rejects China's expansive claim in the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.","\u003cfigure class=\"article-fig size-large\"\u003e\n                        \u003cimg class=\"size-large article-image\" src=\"https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims3/default/strip/false/crop/8640x5760+0+0/resize/1000?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnpr-production-npr.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F69%2F66%2Fe8aba58c4b7a90242b9e7e16a20b%2Fap26321353361028.jpg\" loading=\"lazy\"\u003e\n                        \u003cfigcaption class=\"article-fig-caption\"\u003e\n                            Demonstrators hold signs during a protest against U.S. President Donald Trump's visit to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit and related meetings in Manila, Philippines, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (Firdia Linsawati/AP)\n                        \u003c/figcaption\u003e\n                    \u003c/figure\u003e","\u003ch3\u003eAnti-Trump protesters are gathered in Manila\u003c/h3\u003e","About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump's arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S.","They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, \"Resist U.S. war and plunder!\" They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby.","\"The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines,\" protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press at the Liwasang Bonifacio square, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.","\u003ch3\u003ePlanned meetings with the Philippine president — and possibly an old friend\u003c/h3\u003e","On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries' longstanding treaty alliance.","Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she's well enough and gets her doctors' nod.","Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 \"People Power\" public uprising.","But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: \"How's Imelda?\" Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.","\"Personal connections are very important to him,\" Romualdez said.","When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. \"President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, 'please say hello to your mother,'\" according to Romualdez.","Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.","\u003ca href=\"https://www.npr.org/newsletter/ed\" target=\"_blank\"\u003e\u003cem\u003eCatch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/a\u003e","\u003chr /\u003e","The rise of smartphones in the U.S. coincided with a dramatic slide in K-12 students' reading and math achievement. Now, \u003ca href=\"https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__cepr.harvard.edu_resource_phone-2Dfree-2Dschools-2Dreport\u0026d=DwMGaQ\u0026c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM\u0026r=S4VLcNmpmGywX1ctcW96N0WKo8kqE8ychDvVjnY4H68\u0026m=B64x35o_JYE1iXTJ5E-AeYQYAp_p-HwiosPvwrh4IjDcGNiwE0bZHq8L4Yup9zkN\u0026s=yeHsFGPaemHbCwWM8bame6Ya3H7Xstj4bJZpsvO-6TY\u0026e=\" target=\"_blank\"\u003enew research\u003c/a\u003e suggests putting students' phones in locked pouches during the school day may help restore some of those historic losses.","\"Around 2013, U.S. students started losing 2-3 weeks of learning each year,\" says Harvard University's Tom Kane, one of the new study's co-authors. \"It's been a slow leak that, over time, has put U.S. 8th graders almost a year behind. Strict cellphone bans seem to plug about half of that leak.\"","Or the equivalent of 1-2 weeks of learning a year, according to the study released Tuesday. That's a small but, according to Kane, statistically significant improvement.","\"That could add up over time, just as the initial declines did,\" adds Dartmouth College's Douglas Staiger, another co-author.","The study's authors say it is the first nationwide analysis of student-level test scores in math and reading both before and after schools enforced locked-pouch cellphone bans. It was a joint effort between Harvard's Center for Education Policy Research, Dartmouth and NWEA, a K-12 testing and research organization.","Kane, Staiger and their teams analyzed a nationwide sample of more than 3 million elementary-, middle- and high-school students over the past five school years, comparing the test scores in schools that adopted phone pouches to the scores at similar schools that did not.","Not only did strict cellphone bans appear to trigger small learning gains, the researchers say, those gains didn't seem to fade out after the first year of implementation. Instead, Kane says, the gains appeared to continue, year after year – at least up to three years after adoption.","\u003ch3\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eResearch on phone bans is mixed\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e","Tuesday's headline finding, that locking phones during the school day led to small but statistically significant improvements in math and reading scores, comes with an important caveat:","A \u003ca href=\"https://academic.oup.com/qje/advance-article/doi/10.1093/qje/qjag050/9005628\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eseparate study\u003c/a\u003e, from April, found that these pouches had \"close to zero\" impact on student test scores – and if there was a benefit, it was \u003cem\u003enot \u003c/em\u003estatistically significant.","\"Overall, we didn't find evidence of meaningful achievement gains,\" says Brian Jacob, a co-author of that April study and\u003cem\u003e \u003c/em\u003ea professor of education policy at the University of Michigan.","What should we make of these seemingly contradictory results?","Both are large-scale studies by well-respected teams of researchers. The April study has been peer-reviewed; the more recent study has not.","Both studies similarly focused on schools' adoption of lockable pouches made by the for-profit company Yondr. According to Tuesday's paper, more than 3,300 schools nationwide began using the pouches between the '19-'20 and '25-'26 school years. Typically, schools that use the pouches require that students put their phones in them at the beginning of the day and don't get them back until the end of the school day, when the pouches are unlocked by a school administrator with a special magnetic device.","But the two studies also differ in key ways. The April study pooled school-level mean test scores at several thousand Yondr-adopting schools, while Tuesday's study used student-level scores at the 844 schools that use both Yondr pouches and tests administered by NWEA.","Simply put, the study released Tuesday had more fine-grain, student-level data, but the study released in April was able to examine a much larger sample of schools.","But the two studies' findings also aren't as different as they may seem. Jacob and his co-authors did find statistically significant gains with Yondr pouches in high school math. It's just that those gains were offset by ban-related learning \u003cem\u003elosses\u003c/em\u003e in middle school.","Overall, Jacob says, the new study \"is encouraging. And if [the benefit] really persists and accumulates over time, it really could be a meaningful benefit. I think we'll just have to wait and see if that happens.\"","Another co-author of that April study, Tom Dee, a professor at Stanford University's Graduate School of Education, says of Tuesday's findings, \"I hope they are right that these very small test score gains will aggregate and add up over time. However, I'm not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans.\"","Taken together, Dee says, he considers the results from these early studies into cellphone bans \"largely disappointing,\" and insists \"we need continued study on this topic.\"","Kane sees the results differently. Even if the benefit is small, he argues, relative to the cost – roughly $25 per student – these pouches still make financial sense for schools. \"That's still a lot less than having to pay teachers for an extra week or two of instruction.\"","\u003ch3\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eWhen it all went wrong\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e","For nearly a quarter-century, from 1990 to 2013, math achievement among fourth- and eighth-graders rose steadily. Reading scores also improved.","Then around 2013, student test scores began a sustained tumble that continued through the COVID-19 pandemic and has only recently begun to slow. For years, politicians and pundits blamed pandemic-era school closures for the losses, but the data tells a different story.","\"Particularly in reading, test scores were going down for four to six years before the pandemic,\" Stanford University researcher Sean Reardon \u003ca href=\"/npr/nx-s1-5812483/reading-math-scores-data\" target=\"_blank\"\u003etold NPR earlier this year\u003c/a\u003e. \"In fact, you wouldn't really know there was a pandemic effect if you just looked at the last 10 or 12 years of test scores. There's been just a steady kind of decline regardless of the pandemic.\"","Which raises the question: What happened around 2013?","Possible explanations abound. The federal government began stepping back from holding schools accountable for low test scores. Many schools also saw funding cuts in the wake of the Great Recession.","This new study is the latest to make the case that the mass adoption of cell phones by children and teens also helped fuel those test score declines.","The researchers note that, in 2011, fewer than a quarter of teen students had access to smartphones. By 2018, 95% did. And similar rates in other industrialized countries coincided with similar student achievement declines.","Now, Kane says, he wants to study students' smartphone and social media use \u003cem\u003eoutside\u003c/em\u003e of school.\u003cbr\u003e"],"nprTranscriptID":"nx-s1-10007773-transcript","audio":[{"id":"nx-s1-10007773","audio_length":157,"articleAPIURL":null,"audioAPIURL":null,"org":"npr","orgKey":null,"file_size":2527444,"url":"https://ondemand.npr.org/anon.npr-mp3/npr/me/2026/11/20261117_me_do_school_cellphone_bans_work_new_study_says_yes_but_it_s_complicated.mp3"}],"relatedLinks":[{"id":290517,"url":"/npr/nx-s1-5675979/school-education-kentucky-cell-phone-ban-consequences","prefix":"","title":"What worked and what didn't with a cellphone ban at a Kentucky school","index":1},{"id":290518,"url":"/npr/nx-s1-5812483/reading-math-scores-data","prefix":"","title":"Kids' test scores began declining way before COVID. England Patriots quarterback \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/11/15/lions-35-10-rout-over-patriots-after-maye-injured-in-munich\"\u003eDrake Maye has a right ankle injury\u003c/a\u003e that will sideline him indefinitely, a person with knowledge of the injury told The Associated Press on Monday.","The Patriots are trying to determine whether Maye will require surgery on his ankle, according to the person who spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because the team hasn't addressed the severity of the injury.","Maye stayed in Germany and did not travel back with the team following its loss to Detroit on Sunday for what coach Mike Vrabel said was a decision made “out of caution.”","Losers of two straight games and three of their last four, New England has a bye this week and won’t play again until Nov. 29 when it visits the Los Angeles Chargers.","During his news conference on Monday, Vrabel wouldn't confirm or deny that Maye will be out for an extended period. But he did say he would miss more time.","“I wouldn’t imagine him being available when we come out of the bye,\" Vrabel said.","Maye injured his ankle on a sack by Aidan Hutchinson in the first quarter of \u003ca href=\"https://apnews.com/article/lions-patriots-score-munich-germany-20264a6a48484374747998b186da0a65\"\u003ethe Patriots' 35-10 loss\u003c/a\u003e and didn’t return. Vrabel said after the game that Maye would get tests done once home to determine the severity of the injury.","“He'll be traveling back here shortly, but (the team) just wanted to make sure that everything was good for him to travel back and safely,” Vrabel said earlier Monday during his regularly scheduled radio interview with Boston’s WEEI on the “Greg Hill Show.”","“And it seems like he is.”","The coach said Sunday that he didn’t consider the sack that injured Maye to be improper — Hutchinson had caught up to Maye and pulled him down from behind.","“I’m not going to assume there was something there,” Vrabel said. “However it happened, I don’t think it was anything intentional. I’m sure that it wasn’t. That’s part of the game.”","Backup quarterback Tommy DeVito completed 12 of 24 for 81 yards with one interception and a fourth-quarter touchdown pass to Lan Larison for New England after replacing Maye.","The Patriots managed just 151 total yards on the day, a season low. Philippines — President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.","Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.","The visit marks Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.","As he descended the stairs from Air Force One, Trump pumped his fist. A child handed him small American and Philippine flags, which Trump waved and then swooped in big circular motions as he smiled. The U.S. president was greeted by a marching band playing \"YMCA\" while he walked to a waiting helicopter.","\u003ch3\u003eTrump to be feted at the annual ASEAN summit\u003c/h3\u003e","Trump's first hours in the Philippines will include all the reassuring optics from Washington's oldest treaty ally in Asia, including a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the \"guest of honor\" at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.","The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.","First on Trump's agenda Tuesday is a meeting with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan that have aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific. It will be their first meeting since Trump returned to the White House last year.","Trump is then scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats.","The U.S. had announced a trade framework last October in which Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing U.S. autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. At the time, the Trump administration said Thailand would also spend more than $18 billion on U.S. aircraft and buy U.S. farm goods and liquefied natural gas.","The U.S. Supreme Court overturned in February the 19% tariff that Trump placed on goods from Thailand. The administration sought replacement tariffs in July by levying a 12.5% tax on imports from Thailand for not taking steps to oppose the use of forced labor.","Before the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump will participate in what's billed as a \"special summit\" with the ASEAN leaders, where they are expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region's longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.","Washington rejects China's expansive claim in the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.","\u003cfigure class=\"article-fig size-large\"\u003e\n                        \u003cimg class=\"size-large article-image\" src=\"https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims3/default/strip/false/crop/8640x5760+0+0/resize/1000?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnpr-production-npr.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F69%2F66%2Fe8aba58c4b7a90242b9e7e16a20b%2Fap26321353361028.jpg\" loading=\"lazy\"\u003e\n                        \u003cfigcaption class=\"article-fig-caption\"\u003e\n                            Demonstrators hold signs during a protest against U.S. President Donald Trump's visit to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit and related meetings in Manila, Philippines, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (Firdia Linsawati/AP)\n                        \u003c/figcaption\u003e\n                    \u003c/figure\u003e","\u003ch3\u003eAnti-Trump protesters are gathered in Manila\u003c/h3\u003e","About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump's arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S.","They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, \"Resist U.S. war and plunder!\" They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby.","\"The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines,\" protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press at the Liwasang Bonifacio square, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.","\u003ch3\u003ePlanned meetings with the Philippine president — and possibly an old friend\u003c/h3\u003e","On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries' longstanding treaty alliance.","Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she's well enough and gets her doctors' nod.","Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 \"People Power\" public uprising.","But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: \"How's Imelda?\" Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.","\"Personal connections are very important to him,\" Romualdez said.","When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. \"President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, 'please say hello to your mother,'\" according to Romualdez.","Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Prosecutors have not said if they will retry Clancy on first-degree murder again, or pursue lesser charges.","Clancy's first trial became one of the most widely publicized trials in recent Massachusetts history. Over seven weeks, the trial drew hundreds of spectators to the courthouse, and thousands to the court proceedings' livestream. The trial ignited an international discussion about \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/08/12/massachusetts-lindsay-clancy-murder-children-delusions-maternal-care\"\u003epostpartum mental healthcare\u003c/a\u003e and the cultural expectations of mothers.","During a court hearing Monday at a Plymouth courthouse, prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said that the charges \"require a jury trial,\" but she did not specifically say what charges the district attorney will seek.","Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington said in court that he expects prosecutors will seek first-degree murder charges since that requires a jury trial.","\"The die has been cast,\" Reddington said at Monday's hearing. \"When they say the case is going to require a jury, it's an indirect comment they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments.\"","The Plymouth County district attorney did not confirm that.","Judge William Sullivan set a March 29 trial date.","Reddington argued during Clancy's first trial that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible for killing her three children: 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. Sullivan declared a mistrial in September when jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict.","Clancy's attorneys had asked to dismiss the case after the judge declared a \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/tag/lindsay-clancy\"\u003emistrial\u003c/a\u003e in September. Sullivan \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/11/09/lindsay-clancy-double-jeapardy-motions-denied\"\u003edenied\u003c/a\u003e the request last week.","The defense argued that 11 of the 12 jurors were prepared to find Clancy not criminally responsible for the children's strangulation deaths because she was in a state of postpartum psychosis at the time.","Her attorneys said the judge could have replaced the lone juror who disagreed, and didn't have to declare a mistrial. They said another trial would violate Clancy's rights on double jeopardy grounds — the right to not be tried twice for the same crime.","Sullivan ruled the mistrial declaration was appropriate, and said the court should not interfere with jury deliberations.","During Clancy's trial, Sullivan denied a defense request that could have replaced the holdout juror with an alternate. A single justice of the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court declined to intervene in the case.","The trial captivated public attention and divided public opinion. Groups of women came to the courthouse \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/08/20/hundreds-rally-plymouth-courthouse-support-lindsay-clancy-postpartum\"\u003ewearing pink\u003c/a\u003e as a show of support for Clancy, and sharing their own mental health struggles after childbirth. Meanwhile, some activists and online commenters said Clancy should be held accountable for what they described as the actions of a terrible killer.","Clancy's mental healthcare providers were among the dozens of witnesses who testified. They said Clancy was struggling, and the several medications she was prescribed failed to alleviate her symptoms.","Patrick Clancy, Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/07/29/lindsay-clancy-patrick-clancy-testimony-911-murder-trial\"\u003etestified\u003c/a\u003e that she had called a suicide hotline twice and was released from a psychiatric hospital just weeks before the children's deaths. He and Clancy have filed separate civil lawsuits against her mental healthcare providers, which are ongoing.","Throughout the court proceedings, Clancy has remained at Tewksbury Hospital, where she has been held since 2023."],"enhanced":false,"seriesMeta":null,"iframeHero":null,"postType":"post","isBreaking":false,"isDeveloping":false,"relatedLinks":[{"id":290491,"url":"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/30/clancy-status-hearing-prosecutors-case","prefix":"","title":"Lindsay Clancy is due in court Monday. Maura Healey's Cabinet as the governor gears up for a second term.","Energy and Environmental Affairs Secretary Rebecca Tepper announced Monday that she will depart the administration after almost four years on the job, giving Healey an opportunity to pick a new point person for energy affordability, one of the governor's second-term priority issues. It also means a transition at a time when energy costs are a top concern for residents, the state is struggling to maintain momentum for its policy-backed clean energy transition, and amid debate over whether the state can meet its midcentury decarbonization targets or should backtrack from them.","Tepper's last day is Dec. 4, the administration said, and Healey will appoint Undersecretary for Environment Stephanie Cooper to serve as interim secretary until a permanent successor is named.","Healey called Tepper a \"national leader\" in the field.","\"Secretary Tepper has been a strong advocate for Massachusetts communities, working to protect our natural resources, build resilience to climate change, and advance environmental justice. She has also been a leader among leaders by guiding a northeast coalition of states and Canadian provinces on energy production and transmission. She helped move forward major clean energy projects, including Vineyard Wind and the NECEC transmission line, despite significant federal opposition and cut red tape to bring more solar and storage onto our grid,\" Healey said.","Tepper was chief of the energy and environment bureau in the attorney general's office under Healey and she joined the administration from the get-go almost four years ago. Tepper's departure follows last week's \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/08/28/melissa-hoffer-climate-chief-steps-down-healey\"\u003eexit\u003c/a\u003e by Climate Chief Melissa Hoffer, another day-one Cabinet member for Healey.","\"I've been proud to serve Governor Healey for over a decade, working together to keep ratepayer costs down, standing up for Massachusetts’ energy independence, and protecting our beautiful state from climate change and environmental harm,\" Tepper said. She added, \"In my time in this role, I’ve been laser-focused on building clean energy infrastructure and safeguarding natural resources. I always say the best time to start a new energy project is today. I believe Massachusetts is well-positioned to continue to advance our energy independence in the years to come.\"","Before joining the attorney general's office in 2015, Tepper worked for four years as general counsel for the Department of Public Utilities and was director of the Massachusetts Energy Facilities Siting Board from 2009 through 2011, according to her LinkedIn profile. She worked in the private sector for 15 years as a partner at Rubin and Rudman before joining state government.","Cooper has held a slate of senior roles under the Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs umbrella, having overseen regulatory and policy efforts for clean air and water, solid waste and climate change; guided about $55 million in annual conservation and park development investments; and as DCR acting commissioner led a strategic evaluation that invested in state parks and strengthened core services. She worked in New York City government before moving to Massachusetts.","Asked Thursday about retaining Cabinet members in the administration's second term, and if any secretaries have been asked to make commitments to stay on, Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll said, \"We definitely have an agenda. We want to deliver for the next four years. We want to make sure we have the right people to do that.\"","Healey has experienced significant Cabinet turnover since taking office in 2023, losing the majority of its leadership ahead of this month's reelection. Scientists say the whales continue to struggle from threats including ship strikes and entanglement in fishing gear.","\u003cspan data-index=\"1\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","Marine scientist Heather Pettis, who contributed to the annual report, said the new estimate includes a 11-point margin of error, so  \"it's not the number itself that is cause for alarm.\"","Counting whales often involves uncertainty, she said. The 2024 estimate was increased from 384 to 389 after new data became available.","But, said Pettis,  a senior scientist and chair of the Kraus Marine Mammal Conservation Program at the New England Aquarium, the overall trend is \"worrisome.\"","\"It's that lack of sustained growth, combined with continued injuries and mortalities from entanglements and vessel strikes,\" she said. \"That is what gives cause for concern.\"","Researchers from the New England Aquarium and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration worked together on the annual update.","So far, the 2026 count is looking a bit brighter, due to \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/npr/nx-s1-5670259/rare-species-of-whale-see-uptick-in-births-whats-behind-the-population-boost\"\u003ea record number of babies\u003c/a\u003e born during the 2025-2026 calving season. What we need is for [the calves] to survive to adulthood and then reproduce.\"","Right whales give birth off the southeastern U.S. before heading north to New England and Canada to feed. The carcass of a 4-year-old male named Division was \u003ca href=\"https://www.neaq.org/about-us/press-room/press-releases/severely-entangled-north-atlantic-right-whale-found-dead-off-north-carolina/\"\u003efound off North Carolina in January\u003c/a\u003e following a fishing gear entanglement. Her cause of death remains unknown.","\u003cspan data-index=\"4\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","In addition to the two deaths, there have been eight documented cases of human-caused injuries to right whales this year: seven entanglements and one vessel strike.","Pettis said even non-lethal entanglements can impact a whale's health, ability to reproduce and chances at long-term survival.","The deaths and injuries come amid federal efforts to diminish or delay protections for right whales. Massachusetts group has launched a program aimed at circumventing the Trump administration’s efforts to shut down transgender healthcare for children and teens, and threaten care for adults.","On Monday that effort, a nonprofit called “Project Beacon,” began enrolling patients.","Organizers say they hope to relieve despair among patients and their families as the Trump administration \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/08/12/massachusetts-transgender-care-children-chip-medicaid-hormone-therapy\"\u003eends Medicaid coverage\u003c/a\u003e of transgender care for kids and teens, threatens \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/04/02/gender-affirming-care-massachusetts-baystate-health\"\u003efunding for hospitals\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2025/10/15/fenway-health-medical-care-halt-transgender-children-massachusetts\"\u003ehealth centers\u003c/a\u003e that provide such care for minors and \u003ca href=\"https://www.npr.org/2026/06/12/nx-s1-5855728/transgender-youth-healthcare-trump-subpoena\"\u003esubpoenas some trans children’s medical records\u003c/a\u003e.","In response to these policies, several hospitals and clinics in Massachusetts and across the country have stopped providing treatments such as hormones for patients under 18, and some \u003ca href=\"https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/06/25/2025-11606/patient-protection-and-affordable-care-act-marketplace-integrity-and-affordability\"\u003ehealth insurers\u003c/a\u003e no longer cover transgender care for adults.","“Over the course of the last few years, we’ve seen an unprecedented number of legislative and policy changes that attack the right to access gender-affirming care,” said Nic Tompkins-Hughes, president and board chair at Project Beacon. “We are very lucky in Massachusetts to have the policy, the legislative protection and the funding to stand up a project like this.”","Project Beacon will skirt federal restrictions by refusing all federal funding. Instead, the project will rely on private donations and some state funds. Organizers say they're prepared to serve up to 200 patients a month in the program's first year.","The project will be telehealth only to start, with one part-time physician who will prescribe hormones for patients in transition and puberty blockers for children and young teens. Patients must be referred by their primary care or mental healthcare provider. Project Beacon’s services will be free, for the first year at least, but patients will have to pay for prescriptions.","Max Nash, 17, who scrambled to find a transgender care clinic after Fenway Health closed its program for teens last year, called Project Beacon “awesome.”","“They won’t be able to fill the gap created by the institutions that cut their programs, but it’s better than nothing,” said Nash, who is also a volunteer spokesman for the advocacy group Protect Trans Futures.","Tompkins-Hughes said organizers expect most of Project Beacon’s first-year operating budget, roughly $200,000, will come from private donations. They have requested $75,000 for start-up costs from the state’s \u003ca href=\"https://budget.digital.mass.gov/summary/fy26/outside-section/section-42-affirming-health-care-trust-fund/\"\u003eAffirming Health Care Trust Fund\u003c/a\u003e, administered by the Department of Public Health, and may ask for additional reimbursements. State lawmakers had put $8.5 million into the fund as of July.","Public Health Commissioner Dr. Robbie Goldstein said it’s the state’s job to help residents get the care they need.","“Gender affirming care – like all health care – helps children be healthy, both mentally and physically,” Goldstein said in a written statement. “Children who are affirmed are better equipped to succeed in school, build stronger relationships, contribute more to their communities, and grow into healthier, more productive adults.\"","Advocacy groups and state lawmakers opposed to using taxpayer funds for transgender healthcare expressed anger over the state support for Project Beacon.","\"Hardworking taxpayers expect their money to be spent on essential public services, infrastructure and fiscal responsibility - not on funding controversial medical ideologies,\" said Rep. John Gaskey, a Plymouth Republican, in a statement. \"We must focus on addressing the root causes of psychological distress so individuals can heal and thrive, rather than committing public funds to these treatments.\"","The Trump administration has not responded to a request for comment on Project Beacon, but federal health officials have called attention to the potential for long-term health impacts from taking hormones, which can cause infertility. The administration has also highlighted stories from a handful of people who said they regretted gender transitions. Research shows \u003ca href=\"https://www.americanjournalofsurgery.com/article/S0002-9610(24)00238-1/abstract\"\u003efewer than 1%\u003c/a\u003e of transgender patients regret having surgery related to their transition.","Planning for Project Beacon started in late 2025, around the time U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. called transgender care for kids “\u003ca href=\"https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/hhs-releases-peer-reviewed-report-discrediting-pediatric-sex-rejecting-procedures.html\"\u003emalpractice\u003c/a\u003e” and issued a \u003ca href=\"https://opa.hhs.gov/gender-dysphoria-report\"\u003ereport\u003c/a\u003e claiming science does not support its use. Major medical societies still endorse the care \u003ca href=\"https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/hhs-demands-answers-medical-organizations-sex-rejecting-procedures-minors.html\"\u003edespite threats\u003c/a\u003e from the Trump administration.","At Project Beacon, volunteers considered several ways to continue transgender treatments outside hospitals and clinics before settling on the free care model. Attorneys scrutinized the wording of public statements and websites to avoid \u003ca href=\"https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/07/ftc-requests-public-comment-regarding-gender-affirming-care-minors\"\u003etriggering legal attacks\u003c/a\u003e, reviewed medical and business licensing, liability insurance and the security of medical records.","Some Project Beacon organizers have asked to remain anonymous to protect themselves from professional attacks and death threats.","In its first year, Project Beacon will give priority to children and teens who were at programs that have closed, but adults can enroll too. Patients must be in Massachusetts for the telehealth appointment but can reside elsewhere. The program is prepared to add a second part-time clinician, and may add puberty blocker implants next year if the staff expands to a physical office.","”We’ll reassess after a handful of months when we have a better sense of demand,” said Steph deNormand, Project Beacon’s interim director and director of the trans care program at Fenway Health. “We want to make sure that everyone who needs this care can access it.”","For now, Project Beacon has partners who will assist patients who aren’t comfortable giving themselves shots of hormones or puberty blockers. Health Imperatives, with a network of clinics in southeastern Mass. that offer trans healthcare, is one of those partners.","“There’s always some risk involved in the work we do, especially when healthcare becomes a political lightning rod,” said Stephanie Brown, president and CEO of Health Imperatives, referencing the temporary loss of federal funding tied to abortion care last year. “We will never let politics interfere with the lives of our most marginalized residents, including our transgender community.”"],"enhanced":false,"seriesMeta":null,"iframeHero":null,"postType":"post","isBreaking":false,"isDeveloping":false,"relatedLinks":[{"id":290534,"url":"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/17/southborough-parents-child-gender-transition-court-records-assault-charges","prefix":"","title":"Mass. parents' story about child's gender transition complicated by court records","index":1},{"id":290535,"url":"https://www.npr.org/2026/11/11/nx-s1-6035718/mixed-results-from-ballot-measures-on-abortion-and-trans-issues","prefix":"","title":"Mixed results from ballot measures on abortion and trans issues","index":2},{"id":290536,"url":"https://www.npr.org/2026/09/30/nx-s1-5962843/hhs-study-gender-ideology-flaws-missing-context","prefix":"","title":"What's behind HHS claims that gender-affirming care 'may' radicalize","index":3}],"relatedLinksLabel":"Related:","broadcastType":"","broadcastDate":"","broadcastTime":"","itunesEpType":"","itunesEpNum":0,"itunesSeason":0,"itunesTitle":"","itunesSummary":"","itunesExplicit":false,"socialTease":"In Massachusetts, a group of advocates for transgender health care are opening a free telehealth program for teens and adults who lose access to care. \u003ca href=\"https://makandaproject.com/\"\u003eMakanda Project\u003c/a\u003e’s mission of presenting self-produced, no-cost jazz concerts might be logistically and financially easier if it were a trio rather than a band that starts at 13 pieces, plus occasional guest dancers and string sections.","“But I don’t think we would have built the same following,\" said pianist John Kordalewski.","It’s been the unique model that the group has used for the past 20 years as it has explored the rich legacy of Boston-based composer Makanda Ken McIntyre with both inventive arrangements and exceptional musicianship.","Besides leading the group and writing new arrangements for the hundreds of pieces that McIntyre composed before his death 25 years ago, Kordalewski also works on obtaining grants for the group, which became a nonprofit in 2021. “There’s something unique about the big band, and there are 13 different voices, which makes it more communal,” he said.","\u003cspan data-index=\"1\" data-type=\"youtube\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","A year before the concert series started in 2006, the Makanda Project was born when a group of musicians who were teaching local youth through a New England Conservatory community program played an event that featured McIntyre’s music.","“It seemed too interesting to just do one concert,” recalled Kordalewski, who had studied and played with McIntyre. It also was going to be a tough sell for mainstream jazz clubs. “We realized that if we wanted to have opportunities for a group like this to work regularly — or at all — we had to do it ourselves.”","One early venue, located at a church in Roslindale, asked the band to bring beer for the audience. Some small grants allowed for the beginning of the concert series at the Roxbury Heritage State Park, and in 2008, the band made its debut at the Shaw-Roxbury Branch of the Boston Public Library, which would go on to be its longtime home. (The group also has an outdoor summer series on the lawn of First Church in Roxbury.)","Issues with library program times have meant that recent indoor concerts — like the one coming up \u003ca href=\"https://makandaproject.com/upcoming-performances/\"\u003eon Nov. 21\u003c/a\u003e — have largely taken place at the Twelfth Baptist Church in Roxbury, but Kordalewski expects that at least some of the Makanda events will return to the library this spring.","\u003cspan data-index=\"2\" data-type=\"youtube\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","The band — which includes such important Boston jazz musicians as saxophonist Charlie Kohlhase, bass trombonist Bill Lowe and drummer Yoron Israel — has found continued inspiration from exploring McIntyre’s music. “His compositions are both beautiful but also so creative,” said saxophonist Kurtis Rivers.","Nigerian-born saxophonist Temidayo Balogun pointed out that McIntyre’s Caribbean roots give many of his tunes a calypso feel that echoes West African highlife. “The melodies are relatable to where I’m from, but the harmonies can be so surprising.”","The Makanda Project concerts have often featured significant names from the jazz world like Oliver Lake and Chico Freeman as special guests. In the past, many of the special guests were some of the great elders of jazz — many of them McIntyre’s contemporaries or collaborators.","When Rivers moved to Boston in 1978, he found that Roxbury and the adjacent South End had bustling jazz scenes. For much of the ‘90s, Rivers and Kordalewski played weekly at Connolly’s, a storied Roxbury venue, as members of Salim Washington’s Roxbury Blues Aesthetic.","\u003cspan data-index=\"3\" data-type=\"youtube\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","Now, as it enters its third decade, the Makanda Project is finding that the Roxbury/Dorchester jazz scene it has helped keep alive is showing new signs of renewal. Existing events like Mandorla Music and Greater Ashmont Main Street’s Dot Jazz Series, weekly no-cover jazz at the \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/radioboston/2024/04/02/jazz-music-scene-boston-performance\"\u003eLong Live Roxbury brewery\u003c/a\u003e, and guitarist Fred Woodard’s Dudley Jazz Festival are thriving. Rivers and his own group recently resumed their series at the Ramsey-Toy VFW Post in Dorchester and hope to be back there on a regular basis. And Nubian Square now has a full-time jazz venue in the Jazz Urbane Cafe.","As the organization looks toward its future, the Nov. 21 concert marks a new chapter. The guest is 26-year-old vocalist Brianna Thomas. “I think she’s going to be a very good fit,” said Kordalewski, noting a new generation of collaborators “will have to share our aesthetic, even if they take it in a different direction to some degree.”","The Makanka Project, which has toured Europe and the Midwest and regularly performs in New York, is looking to continue to spread the music of McIntyre to more cities. And locally, it’s been working with groups like Four Corners Main Streets to create a series of events that bring serious big band jazz into everyday life — to street corners or even grocery stores, like the Dorchester Food Co-Op, where they'll return on Dec. 12.","“Those are very unusual places to play jazz,” pointed out Balogun. “People criticize jazz for being too expensive. a clearing on a back lot of the Martha's Vineyard Agricultural Society's property in West Tisbury sits four large trailers. Together, they make up a complete USDA-compliant venison processing facility.","There's a 40-foot refrigerated trailer with racks to hang up to 200 deer prior to butchering. Next to that is where the carcasses are skinned and cleaned. In a third trailer the meat is de-boned, ground, and mixed with beef and pork fat. The result is the venison equivalent of 90% lean hamburger, which is divided into two-pound packages and brought to freezers in the final trailer to await distribution.","The trailers were delivered this fall and, in early November, representatives from the manufacturer, Friesla, came to the Vineyard to help train local butchers to use the modular processor.","Patrick Roden-Reynolds was also on-hand to help with the training. He is the Public Heath Biologist for Dukes County, focusing on tick-borne disease.","\"Tick management and deer management kind of go hand-in-hand in some aspects,\" Roden-Reynolds explained.","Soon, the facility will be accepting deer donated by hunters and producing ground venison for food assistance programs, like the Island Food Pantry which serves one in five year-round residents.","While this solution isn’t new to the Vineyard, it’s taken on a new urgency. Martha’s Vineyard is currently a hotbed for \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/upnext/2026/08/05/alpha-gal-tick-illness-massachusetts-cape-cod-meat-allergy\"\u003ealpha-gal syndrome\u003c/a\u003e – an allergy to red meat and other mammalian products brought on by the bite of the lone star tick. Deer ticks, which spread illnesses like Lyme disease, are also an issue.","\u003cspan data-index=\"1\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","The Vineyard is part of \u003ca class=\"Link\" href=\"https://www.mass.gov/info-details/masswildlifes-hunters-share-the-harvest-program\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\"\u003eMassWildlife’s Hunters Share the Harvest program. \u003c/a\u003eLast year the state began offering hunters free deer permits in exchange for \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2023/11/07/hunters-donate-venison-insecurity\"\u003edonating deer\u003c/a\u003e. And now local nonprofits on both Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket are adding on cash for deer donations.","Roden-Reynolds said the program is starting to take off on the Vineyard.","\"I think in 2022 we had 12 or 15 donations made for the whole year,\" he said. \"And the next year it was like 17 and the next year was 25. And then last year we had a big jump, there was 100 donations made. And this year we're going to break all types of records again.\"","This deer season, \u003ca class=\"Link\" href=\"https://www.tickfreemv.org/hunting-community\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\"\u003eTick Free Martha’s Vineyard is paying $100 per buck and $150 per doe\u003c/a\u003e. The nonprofit also raised the $1.5 million for the new meat processing facility.","\"It's going to help us manage the deer population, which is critical for addressing the tick-borne illness crisis that we're facing,\" said Tick Free MV Executive Director Virginia Barbatti. \"It's also creating a food source for our community and also creating jobs. So there's a lot of reasons that we're really excited about the project.\"","Tick Free MV is handing ownership of the trailers over to the \u003ca class=\"Link\" href=\"https://marthasvineyardagriculturalsociety.org/deer-management-1\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\"\u003eMartha's Vineyard Agricultural Society\u003c/a\u003e. President Lauren Lynch said phase two of the project will involve housing the trailers inside a permanent building. Eventually, the trailers will also be available for butchering livestock.","\"It's a it's a really wonderful example of the way the Vineyard can work together, and once they decide to do something everybody gets on board,\" said Lynch. \"And everyone's been so excited to participate because they see the challenge that all the ticks are posing for the island. And, it's been really exciting to be a part of.”","\u003cspan data-index=\"2\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","It’s a similar story on Nantucket, where the numbers for both food insecurity and deer overpopulation are even higher. According to the nonprofit Nourish Nantucket, one out of every three year-round islanders is food insecure.","A year ago, Nourish Nantucket teamed up with the Nantucket Land Bank to establish the Nantucket Food Hub. It houses the Nantucket Food Pantry, has commercial kitchens and, critically, a butchering space – which allowed them to join the Hunters Share the Harvest program last winter. Nourish Nantucket Executive Director Meg Browers said there are nine times more deer than there should be on the island.","According to state moose and deer biologist Dr. Martin Feehan, the islands have the highest deer densities in Massachusetts. Nantucket, he said, is hovering around 100 deer per square mile in areas open to hunting. The numbers are higher where hunting isn't allowed.","In addition to tick-borne illnesses, that overcrowding also leads to property damage and car-deer collisions.But Nantucket Land Bank Executive Director Rachael Freeman said the Hunters Share the Harvest program is already making a difference.","\"Frankly,\" she said, \"if you’re looking for moving the needle in the right direction, it’s happening.\"","On Nantucket, one-pound packages of ground venison are distributed to clients of the Nantucket Food Pantry, where Ruth Pitts is in charge. She said, while ground venison is commonly mixed with beef and/or pork fat, they use only beef on Nantucket because some of her clients don't eat pork for cultural reasons. Still, not everyone is a fan of the gamey taste.","\"It meets with, you know, some success,\" said Pitts. \"It's just a product literally not everyone's going to take, you know? No matter what your socioeconomic status is, some people eat venison, some people don't.\"","Pitts said she almost always offers venison alongside other protein choices, and about a third of her clients choose to take it home. Even so, she said this fall’s first batch of 167 pounds was gone in two days. And she hopes that continues to be the case as more people learn to incorporate venison into their cooking.","____","\u003cem\u003eThis story is a production of the New England News Collaborative. Generations later, they're coming together again.","bylines":[{"name":"Diane Orson, Connecticut Public Radio","slug":null,"wordpressID":null,"content":null,"apiURL":null,"relativeURL":null,"organization":"wbur","embedMeta":null,"shortBio":"","bluesky":null,"facebook":null,"title":"","type":null,"channels":null,"photo":null,"website":null,"email":null,"nameLastFirst":null,"thumbnail":null}],"nprID":null,"nprTranscriptID":null,"nprURL":null,"dateline":"","superTitle":null,"superTitleURL":null,"content":["Dominique Williams looks out on Bermuda’s turquoise waters. Waves lap against the shore.","As she stands at the edge of St. David's Island in eastern Bermuda, she thinks of her ancestors and the generations of family members who came before her.","\"I think of the struggles that they went through when they came here to Bermuda, when they were taken away from their actual homeland, brought to this small island,\" she said.","Centuries ago, Williams' ancestors arrived on these shores as captives. They were Native Americans, separated from their tribes in New England, enslaved by colonists and shipped across an ocean.","For generations, families in Bermuda passed down stories of their ancestors who had been stolen from a far-away place.","And for generations, families in New England passed down stories of their ancestors who had been sent far away.","About 25 years ago, they found each other — a reconnection centuries in the making.","\"It’s peace,\" Williams said, \"to actually find out who you are. ... It’s being able to know who I am, who my people were, and hold it inside of me wherever I go.\"","\u003ch3\u003eTaking Natives from the land\u003c/h3\u003e","It's an almost-unknown chapter in American history, nearly erased from U.S. textbooks: \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2025/11/28/indigenous-slavery-new-england-bermuda\"\u003eNative American slavery\u003c/a\u003e.","Native slavery in the Americas began in the late 1400s and surged in New England after two wars against Native peoples in the 1630s and 1670s.","In the 1630s, the Massachusetts Bay Colony and the emerging colony of Connecticut wanted to expand into Pequot territory. The Pequot Nation was one of the most powerful nations in the region. When the Pequots resisted, New England colonists – with Native allies – waged a genocidal war to exterminate the Pequots. The Pequot War (1637-1638) led to the enslavement of hundreds of Natives.","King Philip’s War, also known as Metacom’s Rebellion (1675-1678), was a brutal conflict in southern New England between colonists and a group of Native nations. It's considered one of the deadliest wars per capita in American history. Hundreds of Natives were enslaved.","Scholars estimate that around the year 1700, there were as many enslaved Natives as there were enslaved Africans in colonial New England.","Scholars are only beginning to grasp the scope of what happened.","\u003cspan data-index=\"1\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","Ultimately, slavery became a business – a business that helped early colonies pay back debts and fund new settlements, said Mack Scott, a Brown University historian and citizen of the Narragansett Tribe in Rhode Island.","\"New England’s economic system is built within the slave trade,\" Scott said. \"And this lasts until after slavery is over in the United States.","Slavery was also tied to stealing Native land.","\"And it's extremely effective,\" Scott said. \"You’re pushing people out of the centers that you want to be in.\"","Natives from Northeastern tribes were captured, bought and sold. And after the Pequot War, Pequots were also enslaved by other tribes.","Women and children were typically enslaved in New England households. But men could be shipped overseas, sometimes traded for enslaved Africans.","Colonists upended Indigenous peoples’ connection to land that, for thousands of years, was central to Native identity.","\"Native people were extremely afraid of being enslaved, more so a lot of times than dying,\" Scott said. \"Because if you are enslaved and you’re taken from your land, you’re not going to be buried in this place. You’re not going to have those connections to your ancestors and to your children in the future.","\"This was very scary for Indigenous peoples.\"","Enslaved Natives were sent to a variety of destinations, including the Azores, Tangier, France, Bahamas, Barbados, Jamaica, even Mexico. And Bermuda, an archipelago about 800 miles south of New England and 600 miles east of North Carolina.","Bermuda was first colonized in 1609. When settlers arrived they found an uninhabited island. Soon after, it became a bustling center of the Atlantic slave trade. European vessels would stop on their way to the Caribbean.","Once in Bermuda, most enslaved Natives were sent to St. David’s Island. In this remote spot, a unique culture was born. Enslaved Natives intermarried with enslaved and free Africans and Europeans.","\u003cspan data-index=\"2\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","\u003ch3\u003eA mysterious princess story\u003c/h3\u003e","Through the centuries, families passed down stories, generation to generation. For Dominique Williams, the tale of a princess was a favorite, and held a special air of mystery.","\"Possibly that there was some Indigenous woman who was the wife of a sachem or a chief,\" Williams said. \"She and her son were brought to Bermuda. So I remember hearing all of these stories.\"","An ocean away in New England, David Weeden grew up hearing the same stories about Bermuda. Weeden, a citizen of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe in Massachusetts, learned the name of the princess: Wootonekanuske, wife of a renowned Wampanoag chief. His name was Metacom, also known as King Philip. When Metacom was killed, his wife and family were sold into slavery. But no one knew what had happened to his family.","\"One of the variants of the story is that his family were sent to the Caribbean,\" Weeden said. \"And Bermuda was mentioned as a place where they ended up.\"","But there are limited historical records of enslaved people imported to Bermuda. Those that exist can be misleading. That’s one reason why Native slavery is so hidden. For example, Indigenous people were often misidentified as Black.","And in Bermuda, colonists called all Native peoples Mohawk.","\"And repeated it over and over, generation after generation, until the people themselves believed they were Mohawk for a period of time,\" said Michael Thomas of the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation. \"To steal people from their place and their people is one thing. To purposefully prevent them from reconnecting or even understanding who they are is a different level of inhumanity.\"","\u003ch3\u003e'We are somebody'\u003c/h3\u003e","Through the years, Bermuda Natives had lots of questions about where they came from. That included Williams' mother, Lottie.","\"Growing up, we knew we were somebody, but we didn’t know who we were,\" she said.","Lottie Williams remembers being mocked and teased.","\"They would call you names, but you know, you’re children, OK, well, fine,\" she said. \"But as you got older and start to get educated … \"","Her voice trails off and she starts to cry.","\"We are somebody.\"","\u003cspan data-index=\"3\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","When oral histories alone couldn’t answer questions of their origin, people from St. David’s began searching the island’s archives. They found scattered clues hidden in shipping records, maps, paintings and letters.","One example is a letter from 1902 written to American historian Edward Everett Hale. The writer says when her father was a boy in the early 1800s, a formerly enslaved woman told him she was descended from King Philip, the Wampanoag chief who was married to the princess.","Fast forward to the 1990s. The Bermudian Native community was ready for answers, but didn’t think they’d find them on the island. So a group of elders made an unannounced trip to the Mashantucket Pequot reservation in eastern Connecticut.","David Weeden happened to be driving through the reservation on a sunny, hot day and saw the elders walking along the side of the road.","He offered them a lift.","\"We started to have a conversation,\" Weeden recalls. \"They told me why they were here. I told them that my father would be really interested and his name is Tall Oak.\"","His father, Everett \"Tall Oak\" Weeden, was leading the search for Native peoples who’d disappeared into the Atlantic slave trade.","\"And from there, the rest is history,\" David Weeden said.","\u003ch3\u003eCarrying on the journey\u003c/h3\u003e","That chance encounter is now a favorite story shared by families in Bermuda. Dominique Williams believes it was more than chance.","\"You’re telling me you just stumbled upon somebody on the side of the road?\" she said. \"But that’s the universe. That’s Creator trying to bring it back for us.\"","In 2002, Northeast Native communities traveled for the first time to Bermuda to meet their lost tribe and hold a powwow. Years later, they continue to reconnect, as recently as this past August in Connecticut.","\u003cspan data-index=\"4\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","All say finding family has been transformational. It brings Lottie Williams a sense of peace.","\"My mother used to tell we children, 'Remember. You are somebody. You’re related to somebody. So carry on that journey.'\"","Dominique Williams thinks about the stories passed down through the generations on St. David's Island in Bermuda — stories that hinted at a connection to a far-away place.","And now she's able to have a more complete picture of something that her ancestors could only dream about: A better sense of who they are.","\"They fought for us to know about it,\" she said. \"That's why it's still in our stories, in our oral histories. They wanted it to be known for people like me, their descendants, way way way into the future.\"","She said younger generations are on a mission to learn more about their past. They're learning songs and dances. The reconnection allows them to carry on that journey — a journey started by their ancestors.","\"It's just this overwhelming feeling,\" she said.","\u003cspan data-index=\"5\" data-type=\"youtube\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","____","\u003cem\u003eThis story is a production of the New England News Collaborative.
