If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/wburtoday\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\"\u003esign up here\u003c/a\u003e. \u003c/em\u003e","\u003chr /\u003e","The Federal Aviation Administration is still investigating the exact cause of Friday's 4.5 hour nationwide ground stop that resulted in thousands of cancellations this weekend, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. (It was the longest ground stop since Sept. 11, 2001.) But they think \u003ca title=\"it may be related to the FAA's aging telecommunications network\" href=\"https://www.wbur.org/npr/nx-s1-6040952/faa-ground-stop-airplane-travel\" data-linkto=\"https://\" data-cke-saved-href=\"https://www.wbur.org/npr/nx-s1-6040952/faa-ground-stop-airplane-travel\"\u003eit may be related to the FAA's aging telecommunications network\u003c/a\u003e.","The good news is that MassPort said operations at Boston's Logan Airport are expected to return to \"normal\" today. As of 7:45 a.m., Flight Aware showed 34 delays and 13 cancellations in and out of Logan.","Now, let's get to the news:","\u003cstrong\u003eYour other travel plans:\u003c/strong\u003e Thanksgiving is just 10 days away, and for the first time since 2020, AAA is projecting a dip in holiday travel. The agency \u003ca href=\"https://newsroom.aaa.com/2026/11/aaa-thanksgiving-holiday-travel-forecast/\"\u003eannounced today\u003c/a\u003e it expects 81.5 million Americans to travel 50 miles or more for Thanksgiving. That's 121,000 fewer travelers than last year. AAA Northeast spokesman Mark Schieldrop told WBUR's Dan Guzman that higher costs are, in part, \"causing some would-be travelers to pump the brakes,\" even with a recent drop in gas prices. (Friday marked the first time since July 17 that a gallon of regular cost less than $4 in Massachusetts.) Still, with 90% of travelers taking cars to their destinations, traffic is inevitable. Here's when you should head out to avoid the worst of it, according to AAA's latest report:","\u003cul\u003e \t\u003cli\u003eBefore turkey day: AAA recommends traveling before 1 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 24 or before noon on Wednesday, Nov. 25. If you can swing it, there's also minimal traffic expected on Thanksgiving Day.\u003c/li\u003e \t\u003cli\u003eAfter turkey day: You'll want to head out before noon on Friday, Nov. 27, before 11 a.m. on Saturday, Nov. 28 and Sunday, Nov. 29, or before 1 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 30 to steer clear of heavy congestion, according to AAA.\u003c/li\u003e \t\u003cli\u003eWorst times to drive: You'll hit some of the worst traffic in the afternoons and evenings throughout the holiday week. AAA predicts some of the stickiest times to get to your destination will be 2 to 8 p.m. on Tuesday or noon to 7 p.m. on Wednesday. When driving home, try to avoid the windows of 1 to 7 p.m. on Friday, noon to 9 p.m. on Saturday, noon to 8 p.m. on Sunday or 2 to 7 p.m. on Monday.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e","\u003cstrong\u003eContinued coverage:\u003c/strong\u003e Lindsay Clancy returns to court today to determine whether or not she'll face another trial for the strangling deaths of her three children in 2023. WBUR's Deborah Becker reports that prosecutors have not yet confirmed they would retry the case. But if they do, Clancy could be tried for first-degree murder, or prosecutors could opt for lesser charges like second-degree murder or manslaughter, which would allow the defense to ask for a trial without a jury, Deb reports.","\u003cul\u003e \t\u003cli\u003eZoom in: Judge William Sullivan, who declared the mistrial in Clancy’s case this summer, has \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/11/09/lindsay-clancy-double-jeapardy-motions-denied\"\u003ealready denied\u003c/a\u003e the defense's motion to dismiss the case and the prosecution's motion for a gag order.\u003c/li\u003e \t\u003cli\u003eGo deeper: Clancy's defense has argued she should not be held responsible for killing her children because she was experiencing postpartum psychosis. The national conversation surrounding Clancy's case has shone a spotlight on postpartum mental healthcare. Check out Deb's latest below on how some doctors have seen more patients come forward to ask for help in the wake of the trial.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e","\u003cstrong\u003eUplifting the arts:\u003c/strong\u003e The historic West Newton Cinema is gearing up for a major restoration, thanks to a $10 million donation from a familiar benefactor. The same donor who \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2024/05/01/west-newton-cinema-movie-theater-donation-demolition\"\u003esaved the 89-year-old theater from demolition in 2024\u003c/a\u003e is behind the recent multi-million dollar gift, according to a Saturday press release from the West Newton Cinema Foundation, but the benefactor wishes to remain anonymous. The foundation says the cash will go toward a larger $23 million campaign to renovate the space, addressing deferred maintenance, enhancing accessibility and restoring its \"Art Deco elegance.\"","\u003cul\u003e \t\u003cli\u003eOn the to-do list: West Newton Cinema will allot $5 million of the donation to add an elevator, accessible doorways and wheelchair accessible seating in all six of its theaters. Part of the gift will also be used to match funds to entice future donors, according to the press release.\u003c/li\u003e\u003c/ul\u003e","P.S. — \u003ca href=\"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1kIpF-ZoIbk\"\u003eAua!\u003c/a\u003e The New England Patriots' \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/11/15/lions-35-10-rout-over-patriots-after-maye-injured-in-munich\"\u003eSunday game in Munich\u003c/a\u003e ended in a 35-10 win for the Detroit Lions — and an injury for Drake Maye. Weekly Health Newsletter","superTitleURL":"/news/section/health","content":["\u003cem\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eEditor's Note:\u003c/strong\u003e This story was featured in WBUR's weekly health newsletter, CommonHealth. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, \u003ca class=\"c-link elr\" href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/section/health/newsletter\" data-stringify-link=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/section/health/newsletter\" data-sk=\"tooltip_parent\"\u003esign up here\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/em\u003e","\u003chr /\u003e","Poised to take control of Congress in January, Democrats vow that one of their first priorities will be to restore billions of dollars of healthcare funding that Republicans and President Trump cut.","“ We need to lower the cost of healthcare. We need to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits. We need to reverse the cuts in Medicaid,” said U.S. Rep. Jim McGovern, a Democrat from Worcester.","But with Trump still in the White House, the reality is that almost nothing will change right away.","The new Congress will take office in January, just as major healthcare changes start to take effect. Millions of low-income Americans are expected to be \u003ca href=\"https://www.urban.org/research/publication/projected-reductions-medicaid-expansion-enrollment-under-obbbas-work\"\u003ekicked off Medicaid\u003c/a\u003e coverage for failing to comply with new eligibility rules. And \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/onpoint/2025/11/24/aca-subsidies-obamacare-lifeline-for-millions-of-americans\"\u003emillions more\u003c/a\u003e who lost subsidies that help them pay for private health plans \u003ca href=\"https://www.npr.org/2026/11/01/nx-s1-6023423/aca-open-enrollment-health-insurance\"\u003ethrough the Affordable Care Act\u003c/a\u003e will continue to go without that help.","In Massachusetts, up to 300,000 residents are expected to become uninsured because of these policies, \u003ca href=\"https://www.mass.gov/info-details/masshealth-federal-updates-and-impact\"\u003eaccording to state health officials\u003c/a\u003e.","“We are already seeing the harm every day in the form of not only people losing coverage — but being very anxious and very confused,” said Jennifer Lemmerman, executive director of Health Care For All, a Boston-based advocacy group.","She said people who rely on Medicaid should make sure they complete their \u003ca href=\"https://www.mass.gov/federal-changes-affecting-masshealth-medicaid-members\"\u003eapplications for coverage\u003c/a\u003e, even as the balance of power shifts in Washington.","“The election itself doesn't reverse the federal changes already in law,” she added. “I would never want anyone to miss a deadline because they're waiting for what's going to happen in Washington.”","Medicaid programs, which serve low-income residents, \u003ca href=\"https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-launches-statewide-campaign-to-help-masshealth-members-keep-their-health-coverage-after-trump-cuts\"\u003ewill be required\u003c/a\u003e to recheck eligibility for members twice a year, instead of once a year. And many residents will need to prove they are working — or qualify for an exemption — to keep their benefits.","These policies were part of \u003ca href=\"https://www.npr.org/sections/shots-health-news/2025/07/02/nx-s1-5453870/senate-republicans-tax-bill-medicaid-health-care\"\u003ethe 2025 tax and spending legislation\u003c/a\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e \u003c/strong\u003eknown as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” which included nearly a trillion dollars in Medicaid cuts nationwide over 10 years.","\u003cspan data-index=\"1\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","In Massachusetts, Gov. Maura Healey’s administration is spending at least \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/01/28/massachusetts-millions-trump-health-care-policy\"\u003e$30 million\u003c/a\u003e to prepare for the new rules, and \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/08/11/massachusetts-medicaid-masshealth-new-eligibility-rules\"\u003e$10 million\u003c/a\u003e on a public awareness campaign about the changes to Medicaid, which in Massachusetts is known as MassHealth.","Healey, in a statement to WBUR, said she’s hopeful the incoming Congress will reverse healthcare cuts.","“But we need to be clear that the damage is already done,” she said. “Hundreds of thousands of Massachusetts residents are already at risk of losing their healthcare.”","One of the biggest unknowns is how the Republican president will respond to action from a Congress led by Democrats. He could wield his veto pen to thwart their efforts.","“They're not going to have votes to overcome a veto,” said Dr. Benjamin Sommers, a Harvard health economist and primary care physician, who questions whether Congress will be able to pass significant changes to healthcare funding during Trump’s final two years in office.","“If the president decides his role is to block Democratic initiatives, then this will be an election issue for 2028 but won’t actually change before then,” he said.","As more Americans lose affordable health coverage, Sommers predicts a blame game:  Democrats will pin the losses on Trump’s policies, while Trump and his allies will argue the people losing coverage shouldn’t have had it in the first place, he said.","Another question is when and how Democrats will tackle healthcare, including whether they’ll push for incremental changes or a major reform.","\u003cspan data-index=\"2\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","McGovern — who’s in line to \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2018/12/28/jim-mcgovern-house-rules-committee-chairman-me\"\u003ereturn as chair\u003c/a\u003e of the House Rules Committee, which decides the terms of debate on legislation — said lawmakers will try to stop Trump’s healthcare cuts “as soon as humanly possible.”","“We need to, at a minimum, slow them down,” he \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/11/05/jim-mcgovern-congressman-house-rules-committee-democrats\"\u003etold WBUR’s Lisa Mullins\u003c/a\u003e after Democrats' sweeping wins in the midterm elections. “But what our goal should be is to reverse them entirely, because they're immoral.”","Another priority for Democrats is to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies, known as enhanced premium tax credits, which expired at the end of 2025 and resulted in price spikes for millions of Americans. (The fight over the subsidies was also the reason for last fall’s record-long \u003ca href=\"https://www.npr.org/2025/11/05/nx-s1-5596472/government-shutdown-record-health-care-subsidies\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\"\u003egovernment shutdown\u003c/a\u003e.)","Massachusetts relied on \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2025/10/31/massachusetts-health-connector-prices-rise-congress-faq\"\u003e$425 million\u003c/a\u003e in federal funding for these subsidies. The state made up some of the \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/01/08/massachusetts-spending-health-costs-congress\"\u003efunding shortfall\u003c/a\u003e, but not all of it. As a result, \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/02/13/massachusetts-lost-health-insurance-aca\"\u003emany people\u003c/a\u003e dropped coverage because they couldn’t afford the premiums, said Audrey Morse Gasteier, executive director of Massachusetts’ insurance marketplace, called the Health Connector.","“The expiration of enhanced premium tax credits at the end of 2025 was a catastrophic step backwards for health coverage affordability across the United States, and Massachusetts was not immune,” Gasteier said.","The Health Connector serves people who don’t get coverage through their jobs, and earn too much to qualify for MassHealth. Her reporting focuses on mental health, criminal justice and education.\r\n","bluesky":null,"facebook":null,"website":null,"email":"debbmc@bu.edu","content":null,"embedMeta":null}],"nprID":null,"nprTranscriptID":null,"nprURL":null,"dateline":"","superTitle":null,"superTitleURL":null,"content":["When Lindsay Clancy's murder trial began in July, thousands of people tuned into the livestreamed court proceedings. Over social media, they debated whether the mother of three deserved to be found guilty for strangling her children, or should be seen as a victim herself — of a flawed mental healthcare system.","Since the \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/tag/lindsay-clancy\"\u003etrial\u003c/a\u003e turned a spotlight on maternal mental health, clinicians in the field say it's bringing their work out of the shadows. They have reported receiving more questions from both patients and doctors. They've also seen more state funding and want to capitalize on the attention and support to improve the postpartum treatment system.","\"We're in this kind of watershed moment where we need to increase the level of care,\" said Dr. Tiffany Moore Simas, chair of Obstetrics and Gynecology at UMass Memorial Health and a professor at UMass Chan Medical School.","\u003cspan data-index=\"1\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","Clancy's prosecution is still in limbo since the judge overseeing the case declared a \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/04/lindsay-clancy-murder-trial-verdict-massachusetts\"\u003emistrial\u003c/a\u003e in September. A hearing on a potential retrial is scheduled for Monday. Her defense lawyers have argued that mental illness drove Clancy's actions and should shield her from criminal responsibility. Prosecutors have argued that she understood and should be held accountable for her actions.","Studies show that \u003ca href=\"https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/9312-postpartum-depression\"\u003eone in seven women\u003c/a\u003e experience postpartum depression after giving birth. Other conditions, though not as common, include severe anxiety, panic attacks, intrusive or obsessive thoughts and postpartum psychosis. Most of these conditions are temporary and treatable, Moore Simas said, yet stigma remains one of the main obstacles to diagnosis and treatment. New moms may be reluctant to admit they're struggling because of cultural expectations around motherhood, or fear of having their children taken away.","In the wake of the Clancy trial, those fears appear to be decreasing, according to Dr. Uruj Kamal Haider, a perinatal psychiatrist and medical director of the \u003ca href=\"https://www.mcpapformoms.org/?AspxAutoDetectCookieSupport=1\"\u003eMassachusetts Child Psychiatry Access Program For Moms\u003c/a\u003e.","\"I have never seen the stigma of maternal mental health, let alone mental health, be shattered in a way as I have seen in the last couple of months,\" she said.","As the trial was underway, women shared their stories on social media of feeling desperate and alone after childbirth, and many showed up wearing pink at the courthouse in support of Clancy.","\u003cspan data-index=\"2\" data-type=\"pullquote\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","The Massachusetts Child Psychiatry Access Program for Moms, or MCPAP for Moms, operates a helpline for doctors, doulas, social workers and others whose clients are experiencing mental health problems during or after pregnancy. The program's leaders say they've received more questions about how to identify serious postpartum mental health conditions since the trial. They don't yet have data breaking down the types of calls they're receiving.","“What we're seeing is that providers are calling more often worrying that there's just something that they might have missed,” said Dr. Nancy Byatt, founding medical director of MCPAP for Moms and the executive director of the Lifeline for Family Center at UMass Chan Medical School.","Founded in 2014, MCPAP for moms was modeled after a similar program providing advice to pediatricians about children's mental health. It's become a national model for how to help clinicians address perinatal mental health issues. Its helpline fields 300 to 400 calls each month.","The vast majority of Massachusetts obstetricians \u0026mdash; 80% according to the program's leaders \u0026mdash; are enrolled and can access its services. While some physicians have expressed concerns that mental health is not their area of expertise, its leaders point to \u003ca href=\"https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanpub/article/PIIS2468-2667(23)00268-2/fulltext\"\u003estudies\u003c/a\u003e that suggest depression symptoms improved among patients whose doctors consulted the helpline.","Similar programs are now operating in 31 states. Most are state-funded, though some utilize federal dollars.","After the Clancy trial, Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey \u003ca href=\"https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-new-actions-to-strengthen-maternal-mental-health-and-postpartum-care\"\u003ecommitted\u003c/a\u003e an additional $250,000 to MCAP for Mom's $1 million annual budget. The money will be used to train clinicians about perinatal mental health, expand the program to pediatricians, educate families about warning signs and collect statewide data — for the first time — on postpartum psychosis.","Byatt and other mental healthcare providers said shifting the focus of postpartum care would help not just women, but families.","“We have a mental health crisis in our country,” Byatt said. “And I think our best chance of addressing that is to be addressing maternal mental health, because that's how we can break this transgenerational cycle.”","\u003cspan data-index=\"3\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","\u003ch3\u003eSpotting mental health issues earlier\u003c/h3\u003e","Though it is estimated to occur in just one of every 1,000 births, postpartum psychosis is a dangerous psychiatric condition. It surged to prominence because of \u003ca href=\"https://www.npr.org/2026/08/16/nx-s1-5931964/lindsay-clancy-trial-postpartum-psychosis-diagnosis\"\u003ethe role\u003c/a\u003e it played in Clancy's defense. Her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, argued that it caused her to become delusional and hear a voice ordering her to kill her children. He claimed she should not be held criminally responsible for their deaths because of her mental illness.","Prosecutors disputed this. They argued that Clancy killed her children as part of a plan to die by suicide, but was not so mentally ill that she was unable to control or understand her actions.","Postpartum psychosis can be difficult to identify. The symptoms vary but can include increasing anxiety, interrupted sleep, mood changes and becoming disoriented. These effects come and go — something mental health experts call “waxing and waning.” And family members may attribute them to other factors, such as a lack of sleep, hormonal shifts or being overwhelmed as a caretaker.","But Haider said it is possible to recognize these so-called “pink flags” that could signal psychosis, and it's important to catch the signs before they become a severe psychotic episode.","”Postpartum psychosis is a spectrum,” Haider said. “A mom does not need to be actively hallucinating, saying a voice is telling her to throw her baby out the window in order to be psychotic. There are quieter earlier signs and symptoms of pink flags that happen days, weeks, sometimes months before the red flag incident.”","\u003cspan data-index=\"4\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","Haider said more work is needed to educate all medical providers and families about postpartum psychosis and other mental health conditions related to pregnancy. She hopes that with increased awareness following the Clancy trial, more mental health information will be provided to new moms, as well as their partners and loved ones.","Moore Simas, at UMass Memorial Health, has pushed for decades to include mental healthcare as a routine part of obstetric visits during and after pregnancy. Despite statistics that show perinatal mental health issues are common, she said many patients and providers don't know much about them. Moore Simas points out that it wasn't until 2023 that the American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology issued formal \u003ca href=\"https://drive.google.com/file/d/10gs82KjCA-X_ewXoEoD6TJh8M48m0ojY/view?usp=sharing\"\u003eclinical guidelines\u003c/a\u003e for obstetricians to identify and help treat patients' mental health.","Research suggests that women with pre-existing mental health issues are \u003ca href=\"https://www.psychiatrist.com/jcp/risk-factors-for-postpartum-depression/\"\u003emore likely to experience postpartum depression\u003c/a\u003e. Mental health and substance use disorders are among \u003ca href=\"https://policycentermmh.org/maternal-mental-health-fact-sheet/\"\u003ethe leading causes of maternal death\u003c/a\u003e, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and studies suggest many of those deaths could be prevented with appropriate treatment. Haider says serious postpartum mental health problems, like psychosis, are temporary and treatable, but have to be diagnosed early.","“ It truly can happen to anyone, and sometimes when a family least expects it,” Haider said. “And that's why getting at-risk mothers to help as early as possible, even in the pre-conception phase, and talking about preventative women's mental healthcare is so critical.”","\u003ch3\u003eNew treatments arrive\u003c/h3\u003e","The federal Food and Drug Administration \u003ca href=\"https://www.mmhla.org/articles/fda-approves-zuranolone-the-first-oral-treatment-for-postpartum-depression\"\u003eapproved\u003c/a\u003e the first drug for postpartum depression in 2023.","The agency also has approved magnetic pulses to the brain as a treatment for postpartum depression that doesn't respond to other treatments. Small \u003ca href=\"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32056750/\"\u003estudies\u003c/a\u003e suggest this \"transcranial magnetic stimulation\" led to a rapid remission of major depression symptoms in 80% of patients who received it. A clinical \u003ca href=\"https://www.umassmed.edu/news/articles/archives/2025/12/umass-chan-researchers-study-non-drug-therapy-for-postpartum-depression/\"\u003etrial\u003c/a\u003e is underway at UMass Chan Medical School, where researchers hope to enroll 85 participants.","Dr. Kimberly Ann Yonkers, chair of the Department of Psychiatry at UMass Chan and UMass Memorial Health, who is leading the research, said treatments that are not based on medications could address concerns about pregnant and breastfeeding women taking psychiatric drugs.","“This landscape has changed dramatically,” Yonkers said. “So I am very optimistic that we have resources and we have opportunities and treatments that we did not have 10 years ago or 20 years ago.”","\u003cspan data-index=\"5\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","Massachusetts is often rated among the best in the country for mothers and families because of its low \u003ca href=\"https://www.commonwealthfund.org/publications/issue-briefs/2025/jul/maternal-mortality-united-states-2025\"\u003ematernal mortality rate,\u003c/a\u003e family leave policies and many programs to support mothers and children.","But the response to the Clancy trial showed that even educated women with resources, in states with support systems like Massachusetts, can struggle to find effective postpartum mental healthcare. Clancy received multiple diagnoses, was prescribed several psychiatric medications and was committed to a psychiatric hospital just weeks before her children’s deaths. She and her now ex-husband Patrick Clancy have filed separate medical malpractice lawsuits against her former clinicians.","Mental healthcare providers said they will keep advocating for improvements like more training for psychiatrists about perinatal mental health, more mental health screening for new mothers — beyond the usual six-week checkup with an obstetrician — and more education for families and patients about the mental changes during and after pregnancy.","“Massachusetts has been on the leading edge,” Moore Simas said. “We have made progress, but there is still a long way to go.”"],"enhanced":false,"seriesMeta":null,"iframeHero":null,"postType":"post","isBreaking":false,"isDeveloping":false,"relatedLinks":[{"id":290499,"url":"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/01/massachusetts-lindsay-clancy-insanity-defense-criminal-liability","prefix":"","title":"As Clancy jurors remain deadlocked, what to know about the 'insanity defense'","index":1},{"id":290500,"url":"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/08/20/hundreds-rally-plymouth-courthouse-support-lindsay-clancy-postpartum","prefix":"","title":"Hundreds rally outside of Plymouth courthouse in support of Lindsay Clancy","index":2},{"id":290501,"url":"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/08/12/massachusetts-lindsay-clancy-murder-children-delusions-maternal-care","prefix":"","title":"Clancy trial highlights postpartum psychosis and barriers to care for mothers","index":3},{"id":290502,"url":"https://www.wbur.org/upnext/2026/08/05/maternal-mental-health-postpartum-psychosis-clancy-beacon-hill","prefix":"","title":"Advocates push for legislation on Beacon Hill to alter how criminal legal system treats new moms","index":4},{"id":290503,"url":"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/07/20/lindsay-clancy-children-murder-postpartum-trial","prefix":"","title":"Murder trial for Duxbury mom begins. For others, it's a comforting religious or cultural belief. But for researchers at the University of Virginia Division of Perceptual Studies, it's science.","The subject is reincarnation, or the idea that deceased people can be reborn into new bodies. For more than 60 years, researchers at UVA have identified children who, from the time they were toddlers, said they had been someone else. The children proceeded to provide so much detail — almost always familiarity with places, concepts and people they never knew — that researchers were able to pinpoint the deceased person the child said he or she was reincarnated from.","Now, a new study from the center shows that people who died a violent or unexpected death are reincarnated more quickly than others.","Host Robin Young talks to researcher\u003ca href=\"https://med.virginia.edu/clinical/psychiatry-neurobehavioral-sciences/perceptual-studies/dops-staff/saeedeh-sadeghi\"\u003e Saeedeh Sadeghi\u003c/a\u003e from UVA's Division of Perceptual Studies about the center and the new study.","\u003cem\u003eEditor's note: If you have a child sharing past-life experiences, you can reach Sadeghi by email at dopsplm@uvahealth.org.\u003c/em\u003e","\u003ch3\u003eInterview highlights\u003c/h3\u003e","\u003cstrong\u003eYou've said you're not making a statement about metaphysics.\u003c/strong\u003e","\"Yes, exactly. I didn't come to this research with any sort of belief in reincarnation or anything. I was just curious. My co-authors and I do our best to be agnostic and faithful to data and what we observe without jumping into making theories about metaphysics.\"","\u003cstrong\u003eOne child picked out an extra in a photograph from a 1930s Hollywood brochure and told his parents, \"That's me.\" He provided 55 obscure but verifiable facts about a Hollywood agent, including his street name and favorite food. Can you give us more examples of what you're hearing and verifying?\u003c/strong\u003e","\"These are very young children, as you mentioned earlier. Typically, as soon as they can talk, they may start spontaneously talking about what seems like a past-life memory, like a name: 'I had this name. I lived in this place.' A lot of them mention that they miss their old parents, and a lot of them also talk about how they died. A toddler talking about a traumatic death is surprising to a lot of parents.\"","\u003cstrong\u003eThere was a 3-year-old who said he flew a World War II plane off an aircraft carrier called the Natoma Bay.\u003c/strong\u003e","\"James Leininger is a famous case. James Leininger was this Louisiana toddler who began dreaming about being a World War II pilot.\"","\u003cstrong\u003eWhat about what researchers call cultural contamination? Could people who believe in reincarnation be looking for it?\u003c/strong\u003e","\"That's a valid initial reaction, but we're seeing it in American cases also.\"","\u003cstrong\u003eAmong people who don't come from cultures with a strong belief in reincarnation?\u003c/strong\u003e","\"People without much traditional culture that believes in reincarnation. In all cases, when investigators and researchers get involved, they have two goals. One is to see if there is a unique previous person that matches the child's statements, and second, to see if there is any way that the child could have known about this through ordinary processes.","\"Could the child have overheard adults, or did the parents have any motivation to encourage the child to say these things? In many of the cases, we see that there's almost no way the child could have known about this.\"","\u003cstrong\u003eCouldn't parents feed a 2- or 3-year-old this information, show them pictures or coach them?\u003c/strong\u003e","\"Well, it's something to consider, but in many cases, it's just not an explanation. For example, it's not just verbal statements. The child has nightmares or phobias that seem to be related to the memory of the death that they remember.","\"More than half of the children who remember drowning in a past life have a phobia of water, and for a lot of them, the phobia is there even before the child could talk. So it's very hard to imagine that the child could be such a good actor. And a lot of the parents are, in fact, not happy when they hear. Some people freak out. It's not like everyone likes their child to be like this. It's more than just memories. It's behavior also.\"","\u003cstrong\u003eParents report hearing statements like, \"That happened before I was in Mommy's tummy,\" \"You're not my mommy and daddy,\" or \"I died in a car accident.\" These are things you've heard?\u003c/strong\u003e","\"Yeah. There are parents, especially children saying, 'I miss my old parents.' We see in some cases the child insists, 'I want to go and see my old family.' It's something that a lot of the time concerns parents.\"","\u003cstrong\u003eIt could be painful for children who miss another family. Do these memories start to fade around age 7?\u003c/strong\u003e","\"They do. Children usually stop talking about them around that age. Although we don't know if it's fading or if some of them just don't want to bring it up anymore. In general, I think it's probably related to the development of identity. At a very young age, identity isn't still very well-established, and by age 6 or 7, identity becomes much more established.\"","\u003cstrong\u003eLet's go back to James Leininger, the Louisiana toddler who had violent night terrors about a flaming plane crash. By age 3, he said he was a World War II pilot and named a fellow pilot, Jack Larsen. Researchers matched his claims to a real pilot, James Houston Jr., who was shot down over the Pacific in 1945. Do you contact the deceased person's descendants?\u003c/strong\u003e","\"In this case, I think the parents found them through a military reunion. Ideally, we ask the parents not to do it directly, so researchers get involved and independently verify all the statements.\"","\u003cstrong\u003eWhat an emotional bomb for a family to discover a child who knows all these facts about their deceased loved one. How do you approach them?\u003c/strong\u003e","\"When we want to approach these families, it's always hard because we don't know how they react, what their beliefs are and how they feel about it.\"","\u003cstrong\u003eHow do they react?\u003c/strong\u003e","\"It depends a lot on the family. There are some cases who do believe that this is their deceased loved one, and there are cases who don't want to talk or they don't want to think about it. So it's not an easy thing to deal with.\"","\u003cstrong\u003eWhat would you say to people who find this difficult to believe? You told Popular Mechanics that there's a pattern and we should keep looking rather than look away.\u003c/strong\u003e","\"My initial reaction when I first heard about the idea of reincarnation was that this is a religious belief. I don't need to believe in anything.","\"I think I'm just curious, and I invite everyone to be just curious and observe the evidence. Reincarnation is, I think, a filler word for an unknown process. We don't know how it happens. We don't need to jump into making a theory of an afterlife. I don't think we have data to make that theory, but we can just keep looking and observing.","\"This is core to our human identity, our consciousness. Who are we?\"","\u003cstrong\u003eDo you worry about some of these children?\u003c/strong\u003e","\"Yes, I do. I think a lot of these children have what seems like [post-traumatic stress disorder] symptoms from a trauma that they remember from a past life. So I think it's important to understand these children and facilitate these memories in the environments that they are in.","\"A lot of parents contact us with concerns about what to do, and I think more research is needed. How do we interact with these children, and what's the best way to help them? So what we are looking at right now is how these children are different from other children. How is their brain different? How are their cognitive functions different?","\"So it might be that more children have some sort of behavioral or emotional residue from a past life, but these are the children who are capable of talking about it. These children, on average, seem to have advanced verbal skills.\"","\u003cem\u003eThis interview was edited for clarity.\u003c/em\u003e","____","\u003cem\u003e\u003ca class=\"elr\" Yet, that’s what happened to Plymouth resident Irene Olson at the Boston Athenaeum.","Inside the library’s gallery in late October, Olson stood facing a photograph of her 12-year-old self, rolling a baby carriage through the streets of Mattapan.","“ This is our neighborhood store that was called Tony's,” Olson recalled, pointing at the photograph. “This is my friend Linda and my sister Christine, and we used to be mother's helpers, and we would babysit the kids in our neighborhood, and we would take them out for a walk.”","Olson is now among the 29 subjects successfully identified in the Boston Athenaeum's exhibition of Constantine Manos' 1974 photographs, after the \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2025/08/14/boston-athenaeums-photographs-constantine-manos-boston-newsletter\"\u003emuseum began the quest\u003c/a\u003e in 2025. Most of the 29 subjects were identified via social media posts or community engagements prior to the exhibition opening.","Since the exhibition “\u003ca href=\"https://bostonathenaeum.org/whats-on/exhibitions/50-years-later-wheres-boston/\"\u003eWhere’s Boston? 50 Years Later\u003c/a\u003e” opened in June, four additional subjects have been identified, including Olson.","\u003cspan data-index=\"2\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","In 1974, photographer Constantine Manos was on a \u003ca href=\"https://cdm.bostonathenaeum.org/digital/collection/p16057coll59\"\u003enine-month journey\u003c/a\u003e to document life in Boston and beyond for the city’s bicentennial celebrations. That year, he captured 19,000 black-and-white photographs using his 35mm Leica, covering the South End, Mattapan, South Boston, Charlestown, East Boston, Roxbury, the North End, Beacon Hill, Dorchester, Back Bay, Brighton, Brookline and Cambridge.","A second-generation Greek immigrant born in South Carolina, Manos came to Boston at age 19 to become the official photographer for the Boston Symphony Orchestra. He documented Boston, Greece, and cities across the United States, and joined the photography cooperative Magnum in 1963. His work is in the collection of Boston’s Museum of Fine Arts and the Museum of Modern Art in New York, among others. He died in January of 2025.","Manos’ 1974 portfolio and the work of 15 other photographers were displayed in a red, white, and blue-roofed pavilion in front of the Prudential Center in 1975. The exhibition was titled “Where’s Boston?” and ran through 1978. Olson visited the show several times as a teenager, when her image was also featured.","Earlier this year, Olson noticed “Where’s Boston? 50 Years Later” in an online event listing, and recognized the title from the bicentennial. She visited in person and encountered her image again.","\u003cspan data-index=\"3\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","“ It was exciting, you know? And not only that, but it's like a piece of your history,” said Olson. “This was your neighborhood that you grew up in and even to this day, there's so much nostalgia just looking at this.”","Olson returned to the exhibit on Oct. 30 to conduct an oral history interview with associate curator Lauren Graves. The museum has collected 17 oral histories since 2025, 12 of which are included in the exhibition.","Olson didn’t remember her interaction with Manos, but remembers the photo being taken. Standing in front of the photo with Graves, she recounted details from her adolescence, like working at Rico’s Market, her childhood dog (who is featured in the photo), and the riots and tensions that arose from the busing crisis in the 1970s.","Olson is a third-generation Bostonian who grew up in Mattapan. After getting married, she moved to Milton, then raised her two daughters in Duxbury. She now lives in Plymouth and works as a part-time harbormaster.","“ There's a strong connection to Boston throughout our lives,” said Olson. “ Boston's something that's in your blood, I believe, you know? And if you were born here, there's a sense of pride that goes with it.”","\u003cspan data-index=\"4\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","Since the exhibition opened, Graves said that three more people have identified themselves or others in the photographs:  a dancer at the Elma Lewis School of Fine Arts in Roxbury, a son who recognized his father dressed as a mime, and a neighbor who identified her local fireman.","All of the oral histories will be \u003ca href=\"https://cdm.bostonathenaeum.org/digital/collection/p16057coll16/search/searchterm/%E2%80%9Cwhere's%20boston%3F%2050%20years%20later%E2%80%9D%20oral%20histories/field/collec/mode/exact/conn/and\"\u003earchived\u003c/a\u003e on the Boston Athenaeum website.”","Even when the exhibition closes on Dec. 12, Graves hopes to continue to ID subjects in \u003ca href=\"https://cdm.bostonathenaeum.org/digital/collection/p16057coll59/search\"\u003eManos’ photographs\u003c/a\u003e. She invites visitors to look through the collection and identify themselves or others.","Graves says she has been impressed by the openness and generosity of those sharing their stories.","“I assumed we would talk about the photo, and no one really wanted to talk about the photograph necessarily,” said Graves. “They wanted to talk about the stores around it, the street, their family home. The photograph is just a small part that tells this much larger Massachusetts group has launched a program aimed at circumventing the Trump administration’s efforts to shut down transgender healthcare for children and teens, and threaten care for adults.","On Monday that effort, a nonprofit called “Project Beacon,” began enrolling patients.","Organizers say they hope to relieve despair among patients and their families as the Trump administration \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/08/12/massachusetts-transgender-care-children-chip-medicaid-hormone-therapy\"\u003eends Medicaid coverage\u003c/a\u003e of transgender care for kids and teens, threatens \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/04/02/gender-affirming-care-massachusetts-baystate-health\"\u003efunding for hospitals\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2025/10/15/fenway-health-medical-care-halt-transgender-children-massachusetts\"\u003ehealth centers\u003c/a\u003e that provide such care for minors and \u003ca href=\"https://www.npr.org/2026/06/12/nx-s1-5855728/transgender-youth-healthcare-trump-subpoena\"\u003esubpoenas some trans children’s medical records\u003c/a\u003e.","In response to these policies, several hospitals and clinics in Massachusetts and across the country have stopped providing treatments such as hormones for patients under 18, and some \u003ca href=\"https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/06/25/2025-11606/patient-protection-and-affordable-care-act-marketplace-integrity-and-affordability\"\u003ehealth insurers\u003c/a\u003e no longer cover transgender care for adults.","“Over the course of the last few years, we’ve seen an unprecedented number of legislative and policy changes that attack the right to access gender-affirming care,” said Nic Tompkins-Hughes, president and board chair at Project Beacon. “We are very lucky in Massachusetts to have the policy, the legislative protection and the funding to stand up a project like this.”","Project Beacon will skirt federal restrictions by refusing all federal funding. Instead, the project will rely on private donations and some state funds. Organizers say they're prepared to serve up to 200 patients a month in the program's first year.","The project will be telehealth only to start, with one part-time physician who will prescribe hormones for patients in transition and puberty blockers for children and young teens. Patients must be referred by their primary care or mental healthcare provider. Project Beacon’s services will be free, for the first year at least, but patients will have to pay for prescriptions.","Max Nash, 17, who scrambled to find a transgender care clinic after Fenway Health closed its program for teens last year, called Project Beacon “awesome.”","“They won’t be able to fill the gap created by the institutions that cut their programs, but it’s better than nothing,” said Nash, who is also a volunteer spokesman for the advocacy group Protect Trans Futures.","Tompkins-Hughes said organizers expect most of Project Beacon’s first-year operating budget, roughly $200,000, will come from private donations. They have requested $75,000 for start-up costs from the state’s \u003ca href=\"https://budget.digital.mass.gov/summary/fy26/outside-section/section-42-affirming-health-care-trust-fund/\"\u003eAffirming Health Care Trust Fund\u003c/a\u003e, administered by the Department of Public Health, and may ask for additional reimbursements. State lawmakers had put $8.5 million into the fund as of July.","Public Health Commissioner Dr. Robbie Goldstein said it’s the state’s job to help residents get the care they need.","“Gender affirming care – like all health care – helps children be healthy, both mentally and physically,” Goldstein said in a written statement. “Children who are affirmed are better equipped to succeed in school, build stronger relationships, contribute more to their communities, and grow into healthier, more productive adults.\"","Advocacy groups and state lawmakers opposed to using taxpayer funds for transgender healthcare expressed anger over the state support for Project Beacon.","\"Hardworking taxpayers expect their money to be spent on essential public services, infrastructure and fiscal responsibility - not on funding controversial medical ideologies,\" said Rep. John Gaskey, a Plymouth Republican, in a statement. \"We must focus on addressing the root causes of psychological distress so individuals can heal and thrive, rather than committing public funds to these treatments.\"","The Trump administration has not responded to a request for comment on Project Beacon, but federal health officials have called attention to the potential for long-term health impacts from taking hormones, which can cause infertility. The administration has also highlighted stories from a handful of people who said they regretted gender transitions. Research shows \u003ca href=\"https://www.americanjournalofsurgery.com/article/S0002-9610(24)00238-1/abstract\"\u003efewer than 1%\u003c/a\u003e of transgender patients regret having surgery related to their transition.","Planning for Project Beacon started in late 2025, around the time U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. called transgender care for kids “\u003ca href=\"https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/hhs-releases-peer-reviewed-report-discrediting-pediatric-sex-rejecting-procedures.html\"\u003emalpractice\u003c/a\u003e” and issued a \u003ca href=\"https://opa.hhs.gov/gender-dysphoria-report\"\u003ereport\u003c/a\u003e claiming science does not support its use. Major medical societies still endorse the care \u003ca href=\"https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/hhs-demands-answers-medical-organizations-sex-rejecting-procedures-minors.html\"\u003edespite threats\u003c/a\u003e from the Trump administration.","At Project Beacon, volunteers considered several ways to continue transgender treatments outside hospitals and clinics before settling on the free care model. Attorneys scrutinized the wording of public statements and websites to avoid \u003ca href=\"https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/07/ftc-requests-public-comment-regarding-gender-affirming-care-minors\"\u003etriggering legal attacks\u003c/a\u003e, reviewed medical and business licensing, liability insurance and the security of medical records.","Some Project Beacon organizers have asked to remain anonymous to protect themselves from professional attacks and death threats.","In its first year, Project Beacon will give priority to children and teens who were at programs that have closed, but adults can enroll too. Patients must be in Massachusetts for the telehealth appointment but can reside elsewhere. The program is prepared to add a second part-time clinician, and may add puberty blocker implants next year if the staff expands to a physical office.","”We’ll reassess after a handful of months when we have a better sense of demand,” said Steph deNormand, Project Beacon’s interim director and director of the trans care program at Fenway Health. “We want to make sure that everyone who needs this care can access it.”","For now, Project Beacon has partners who will assist patients who aren’t comfortable giving themselves shots of hormones or puberty blockers. Health Imperatives, with a network of clinics in southeastern Mass. that offer trans healthcare, is one of those partners.","“There’s always some risk involved in the work we do, especially when healthcare becomes a political lightning rod,” said Stephanie Brown, president and CEO of Health Imperatives, referencing the temporary loss of federal funding tied to abortion care last year. “We will never let politics interfere with the lives of our most marginalized residents, including our transgender community.”"],"enhanced":false,"seriesMeta":null,"iframeHero":null,"postType":"post","isBreaking":false,"isDeveloping":false,"relatedLinks":[{"url":"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/17/southborough-parents-child-gender-transition-court-records-assault-charges","title":"Mass. parents' story about child's gender transition complicated by court records","prefix":""},{"url":"https://www.npr.org/2026/11/11/nx-s1-6035718/mixed-results-from-ballot-measures-on-abortion-and-trans-issues","title":"Mixed results from ballot measures on abortion and trans issues","prefix":""},{"url":"https://www.npr.org/2026/09/30/nx-s1-5962843/hhs-study-gender-ideology-flaws-missing-context","title":"What's behind HHS claims that gender-affirming care 'may' radicalize","prefix":""}],"relatedLinksLabel":"Related:","broadcastType":"","broadcastDate":"","broadcastTime":"","itunesEpType":"","itunesEpNum":0,"itunesSeason":0,"itunesTitle":"","itunesSummary":"","itunesExplicit":false,"socialTease":"In Massachusetts, a group of advocates for transgender health care are opening a free telehealth program for teens and adults who lose access to care. team.","bluesky":null,"facebook":null,"website":null,"email":null,"content":null,"embedMeta":null}],"nprID":null,"nprTranscriptID":null,"nprURL":null,"dateline":"","superTitle":null,"superTitleURL":null,"content":["Housing advocates in Massachusetts are decrying a new move from the Trump administration to require all people living in federally-subsidized public housing to prove their U.S. citizenship or legal immigration status.","Advocates say the move could displace thousands of people in mixed-status immigration households, even if family members have legal status since they may be fearful of sharing information with the federal government due to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.","\"They are going to be separated, or they have to self-evict,\" said Zafiro Patiño, director of organizing for the Massachusetts Union of Public Housing Tenants. \"That's what we are hearing mainly — that people are going to be afraid of actually revealing these documents, and they are going to self-evict.\"","The \u003ca href=\"https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/12/2026-23003/housing-and-community-development-act-of-1980-verification-of-eligible-status\"\u003erule\u003c/a\u003e, issued last Thursday by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, would require all tenants who live in federally-funded housing to show proof of U.S. citizenship or lawful immigration status. It goes into effect on Dec. 15 and tenants must submit proof of status by March 14.","Since 1995, federal policy has allowed mixed-status families to live together in HUD-assisted housing. The government only provides rental assistance to eligible family members, and families pay a higher, pro-rated share of rent.","The Trump administration's new rule would eliminate that arrangement. Advocates say it would potentially force families to choose between remaining together outside public housing or separating so eligible household members can retain assistance.","\"We believe that a lot of people are going to be displaced,\" Patiño said. \"It's very tragic because it's going to divide families.\"","In a statement \u003ca href=\"https://www.hud.gov/news/hud-no-26-091\"\u003eonline\u003c/a\u003e, Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner has said the agency is implementing the rule because it wants to ensure only citizens and eligible immigrants live in federally-subsidized housing.","It cited the long waiting lists for the housing as a reason to further inspect tenants.","“It’s unacceptable that America’s homeless veterans, disabled, elderly, and victims of domestic violence languish on waitlists while illegals and ineligibles scam our system. American taxpayers will no longer foot the bill. Promises made, promises kept,” Turner said.","The office claims it and the Department of Homeland Security audited the agency and found nearly 200,000 tenants who had incomplete or unknown eligibility verification.","The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan research institute, estimates that nearly \u003ca href=\"https://www.cbpp.org/sites/default/files/12-12-25hous.pdf\"\u003e1,000 households\u003c/a\u003e in Massachusetts would be affected by the change. The center also finds Massachusetts would have the fourth-highest number of affected households, behind California, New York and Texas.","The administration had attempted to implement similar requirements in 2019 and reintroduced the proposal this past February.","A coalition of 22 state attorneys general, including Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell, sent \u003ca About 50 objects from her archive will bedazzle the Museum of Fine Arts this spring, including her blood-red Alberta Ferretti gown and her green Gibson J-180 acoustic guitar.","“Taylor Swift: The Eras Collection,” opens April 10, 2027 and brings the artistry and spectacle of her “Eras Tour” to the gallery. It’s the first exhibition in the MFA’s history dedicated solely to a musician and the archive’s only stop.","Kristen Hoskins, director of public programs, co-curated what promises to be a blockbuster show. In an announcement on Tuesday she said the MFA is inviting visitors to take an intimate look at the fashion and instruments of one of today’s most influential cultural figures.","\"I'm excited to welcome audiences across generations to this unique experience at the Museum,” Hoskins said, “especially Swifties, whose passion and community building are an essential part of Taylor's story.\"","\u003cspan data-index=\"1\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","The Eras Tour grossed more than $2 billion in ticket sales. Like the tour, the exhibition spans Swift’s 20-year career, from her self-titled 2006 debut album to 2025’s “The Life of a Showgirl.” Vignettes built around “Tim McGraw” (2006) and “The Fate of Ophelia” (2025) bookend the museum’s exhibition.","Other highlights include Swift’s midnight-blue, crystal-laden Zuhair Murad bodysuit, the Deering banjo from her Broadway-inspired “Speak Now” world tour and the mandolin she played in the 2020 video for “Willow” and the typewriter seen in her 2024 video for “Fortnight.”","\"With over a century of experience celebrating the art of musical instruments and fashion, the MFA is the perfect place to host an exhibition exploring Taylor Swift's exceptional artistry,\" Jared Katz, curator of musical instruments, said in the announcement. \"I'm delighted that we are able to make accessible these instruments and costumes from all of Taylor’s eras, which represent a remarkable musical journey across genres over the last 20 years.”","Katz said he hopes visitors leave with a deeper appreciation for Swift’s creativity and talent, “and maybe even get inspired to start creating music of their own.\"","Timed tickets cost $40 and go on sale to the public at 6 p.m. on Dec. 13, which is Swift’s 37th birthday. CAI","slug":null,"wordpressID":null,"content":null,"apiURL":null,"relativeURL":null,"organization":"wbur","embedMeta":null,"shortBio":"","bluesky":null,"facebook":null,"title":"","type":null,"channels":null,"photo":null,"website":null,"email":null,"nameLastFirst":null,"thumbnail":null}],"nprID":null,"nprTranscriptID":null,"nprURL":null,"dateline":"","superTitle":null,"superTitleURL":null,"content":["In a clearing on a back lot of the Martha's Vineyard Agricultural Society's property in West Tisbury sits four large trailers. Together, they make up a complete USDA-compliant venison processing facility.","There's a 40-foot refrigerated trailer with racks to hang up to 200 deer prior to butchering. Next to that is where the carcasses are skinned and cleaned. In a third trailer the meat is de-boned, ground, and mixed with beef and pork fat. The result is the venison equivalent of 90% lean hamburger, which is divided into two-pound packages and brought to freezers in the final trailer to await distribution.","The trailers were delivered this fall and, in early November, representatives from the manufacturer, Friesla, came to the Vineyard to help train local butchers to use the modular processor.","Patrick Roden-Reynolds was also on-hand to help with the training. He is the Public Heath Biologist for Dukes County, focusing on tick-borne disease.","\"Tick management and deer management kind of go hand-in-hand in some aspects,\" Roden-Reynolds explained.","Soon, the facility will be accepting deer donated by hunters and producing ground venison for food assistance programs, like the Island Food Pantry which serves one in five year-round residents.","While this solution isn’t new to the Vineyard, it’s taken on a new urgency. Martha’s Vineyard is currently a hotbed for \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/upnext/2026/08/05/alpha-gal-tick-illness-massachusetts-cape-cod-meat-allergy\"\u003ealpha-gal syndrome\u003c/a\u003e – an allergy to red meat and other mammalian products brought on by the bite of the lone star tick. Deer ticks, which spread illnesses like Lyme disease, are also an issue.","\u003cspan data-index=\"1\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","The Vineyard is part of \u003ca class=\"Link\" href=\"https://www.mass.gov/info-details/masswildlifes-hunters-share-the-harvest-program\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\"\u003eMassWildlife’s Hunters Share the Harvest program. \u003c/a\u003eLast year the state began offering hunters free deer permits in exchange for \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2023/11/07/hunters-donate-venison-insecurity\"\u003edonating deer\u003c/a\u003e. And now local nonprofits on both Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket are adding on cash for deer donations.","Roden-Reynolds said the program is starting to take off on the Vineyard.","\"I think in 2022 we had 12 or 15 donations made for the whole year,\" he said. \"And the next year it was like 17 and the next year was 25. And then last year we had a big jump, there was 100 donations made. And this year we're going to break all types of records again.\"","This deer season, \u003ca class=\"Link\" href=\"https://www.tickfreemv.org/hunting-community\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\"\u003eTick Free Martha’s Vineyard is paying $100 per buck and $150 per doe\u003c/a\u003e. The nonprofit also raised the $1.5 million for the new meat processing facility.","\"It's going to help us manage the deer population, which is critical for addressing the tick-borne illness crisis that we're facing,\" said Tick Free MV Executive Director Virginia Barbatti. \"It's also creating a food source for our community and also creating jobs. So there's a lot of reasons that we're really excited about the project.\"","Tick Free MV is handing ownership of the trailers over to the \u003ca class=\"Link\" href=\"https://marthasvineyardagriculturalsociety.org/deer-management-1\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\"\u003eMartha's Vineyard Agricultural Society\u003c/a\u003e. President Lauren Lynch said phase two of the project will involve housing the trailers inside a permanent building. Eventually, the trailers will also be available for butchering livestock.","\"It's a it's a really wonderful example of the way the Vineyard can work together, and once they decide to do something everybody gets on board,\" said Lynch. \"And everyone's been so excited to participate because they see the challenge that all the ticks are posing for the island. And, it's been really exciting to be a part of.”","\u003cspan data-index=\"2\" data-type=\"caption\"\u003e\u003c/span\u003e","It’s a similar story on Nantucket, where the numbers for both food insecurity and deer overpopulation are even higher. According to the nonprofit Nourish Nantucket, one out of every three year-round islanders is food insecure.","A year ago, Nourish Nantucket teamed up with the Nantucket Land Bank to establish the Nantucket Food Hub. It houses the Nantucket Food Pantry, has commercial kitchens and, critically, a butchering space – which allowed them to join the Hunters Share the Harvest program last winter. Nourish Nantucket Executive Director Meg Browers said there are nine times more deer than there should be on the island.","According to state moose and deer biologist Dr. Martin Feehan, the islands have the highest deer densities in Massachusetts. Nantucket, he said, is hovering around 100 deer per square mile in areas open to hunting. The numbers are higher where hunting isn't allowed.","In addition to tick-borne illnesses, that overcrowding also leads to property damage and car-deer collisions.But Nantucket Land Bank Executive Director Rachael Freeman said the Hunters Share the Harvest program is already making a difference.","\"Frankly,\" she said, \"if you’re looking for moving the needle in the right direction, it’s happening.\"","On Nantucket, one-pound packages of ground venison are distributed to clients of the Nantucket Food Pantry, where Ruth Pitts is in charge. She said, while ground venison is commonly mixed with beef and/or pork fat, they use only beef on Nantucket because some of her clients don't eat pork for cultural reasons. Still, not everyone is a fan of the gamey taste.","\"It meets with, you know, some success,\" said Pitts. \"It's just a product literally not everyone's going to take, you know? No matter what your socioeconomic status is, some people eat venison, some people don't.\"","Pitts said she almost always offers venison alongside other protein choices, and about a third of her clients choose to take it home. Even so, she said this fall’s first batch of 167 pounds was gone in two days. And she hopes that continues to be the case as more people learn to incorporate venison into their cooking.","____","\u003cem\u003eThis story is a production of the New England News Collaborative. Maura Healey's Cabinet as the governor gears up for a second term.","Energy and Environmental Affairs Secretary Rebecca Tepper announced Monday that she will depart the administration after almost four years on the job, giving Healey an opportunity to pick a new point person for energy affordability, one of the governor's second-term priority issues. It also means a transition at a time when energy costs are a top concern for residents, the state is struggling to maintain momentum for its policy-backed clean energy transition, and amid debate over whether the state can meet its midcentury decarbonization targets or should backtrack from them.","Tepper's last day is Dec. 4, the administration said, and Healey will appoint Undersecretary for Environment Stephanie Cooper to serve as interim secretary until a permanent successor is named.","Healey called Tepper a \"national leader\" in the field.","\"Secretary Tepper has been a strong advocate for Massachusetts communities, working to protect our natural resources, build resilience to climate change, and advance environmental justice. She has also been a leader among leaders by guiding a northeast coalition of states and Canadian provinces on energy production and transmission. She helped move forward major clean energy projects, including Vineyard Wind and the NECEC transmission line, despite significant federal opposition and cut red tape to bring more solar and storage onto our grid,\" Healey said.","Tepper was chief of the energy and environment bureau in the attorney general's office under Healey and she joined the administration from the get-go almost four years ago. Tepper's departure follows last week's \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/08/28/melissa-hoffer-climate-chief-steps-down-healey\"\u003eexit\u003c/a\u003e by Climate Chief Melissa Hoffer, another day-one Cabinet member for Healey.","\"I've been proud to serve Governor Healey for over a decade, working together to keep ratepayer costs down, standing up for Massachusetts’ energy independence, and protecting our beautiful state from climate change and environmental harm,\" Tepper said. She added, \"In my time in this role, I’ve been laser-focused on building clean energy infrastructure and safeguarding natural resources. I always say the best time to start a new energy project is today. I believe Massachusetts is well-positioned to continue to advance our energy independence in the years to come.\"","Before joining the attorney general's office in 2015, Tepper worked for four years as general counsel for the Department of Public Utilities and was director of the Massachusetts Energy Facilities Siting Board from 2009 through 2011, according to her LinkedIn profile. She worked in the private sector for 15 years as a partner at Rubin and Rudman before joining state government.","Cooper has held a slate of senior roles under the Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs umbrella, having overseen regulatory and policy efforts for clean air and water, solid waste and climate change; guided about $55 million in annual conservation and park development investments; and as DCR acting commissioner led a strategic evaluation that invested in state parks and strengthened core services. She worked in New York City government before moving to Massachusetts.","Asked Thursday about retaining Cabinet members in the administration's second term, and if any secretaries have been asked to make commitments to stay on, Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll said, \"We definitely have an agenda. We want to deliver for the next four years. We want to make sure we have the right people to do that.\"","Healey has experienced significant Cabinet turnover since taking office in 2023, losing the majority of its leadership ahead of this month's reelection. Committee to Restrict Data Centers announced a campaign Thursday to put new restrictions before Massachusetts voters in 2028. The announcement came after news that the Kraft Group is pursuing a data center campus in Sutton that, if completed, would rank as the fourth-largest in the country.","bylines":[{"name":"Sam Drysdale, State House News Service","slug":null,"wordpressID":null,"content":null,"apiURL":null,"relativeURL":null,"organization":"wbur","embedMeta":null,"shortBio":"","bluesky":null,"facebook":null,"title":"","type":null,"channels":null,"photo":null,"website":null,"email":null,"nameLastFirst":null,"thumbnail":null}],"nprID":null,"nprTranscriptID":null,"nprURL":null,"dateline":"","superTitle":null,"superTitleURL":null,"content":["Opponents of data center development have launched a campaign to put new restrictions before Massachusetts voters in 2028, as a $16 billion project proposed in Sutton sharpens the debate.","The Committee to Restrict Data Centers, which filed initial paperwork with state regulators in September, announced the campaign Thursday and launched \u003ca href=\"http://sign4restrictingdatacenters.org/\"\u003esign4restrictingdatacenters.org\u003c/a\u003e, where residents can pledge support for a ballot petition and request a signature form by mail.","The Kraft Group is pursuing a \u003ca href=\"https://www.cbsnews.com/boston/news/sutton-data-center-campus-kraft/\"\u003edata center campus in Sutton\u003c/a\u003e that, if completed, would rank as the \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/22/new-england-ai-data-centers-explainer\"\u003efourth-largest data center in the country\u003c/a\u003e. The proposal has drawn opposition from residents of the central Massachusetts town, adding to the unfolding \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/npr/nx-s1-5927288/data-center-election-voters-ai\"\u003enational debate over AI development\u003c/a\u003e, electricity consumption, water use and potential effects on utility bills.","The website urges visitors to help restrict data centers, citing concerns about increasing electric bills, water consumption and noise from equipment that can \"sound like jet engines.\" It also calls for local voter approval of proposed facilities. At the bottom of the site, organizers included a declaration: \"No Ai was used on this site.\"","The committee's proposal, designated Petition 26-08 by the attorney general's office, would establish requirements for new data centers and expansions of existing facilities, including a two-thirds vote of approval by residents in the host community.","Under the petition, a data center could not receive a municipal permit unless its electricity supplier agreed not to shift costs onto other customers and committed to providing enough electricity from 100% renewable resources to meet the facility's needs without reducing renewable energy available to others. Operators would also have to guarantee recovery of infrastructure costs if a facility closes, reduces capacity or violates its contract.","The proposal also requires water suppliers to certify that existing systems can accommodate a facility without materially affecting service to existing customers in the host or neighboring communities. Operators would need drought-related water reduction plans.","Municipalities would have to publicly disclose permitting documents online, and voters would decide whether to approve a proposed facility at an election at least 180 days after the community announces its permitting decision and releases the relevant documents. The state auditor could audit data centers and their electricity and water suppliers, with municipalities authorized to require facilities to cease operating until certain violations are corrected.","The committee is chaired by Jim Fleming, a political consultant who operates a signature-gathering company and said he has connections to communities that have raised concerns about data center projects, including Westfield and Holyoke.","Sen. John Velis, a Westfield Democrat, is also promoting the campaign.","\"The completion and proposed construction of data centers around the state has caused local community groups to organize to either stop or delay new centers,\" Velis said in the committee's press release, citing concerns about electricity costs, environmental uncertainty, water usage and noise.","Fleming submitted the proposal shortly before this year's August filing deadline, and Attorney General Andrea Campbell's office certified it in September.","The committee is not planning to collect signatures for the first available deadline this month, Fleming said. Organizers have until Nov. 18 to submit 74,574 signatures, representing 3% of the votes cast in the 2022 gubernatorial election, to qualify for the next stage of the process. Because the proposal is intended for the 2028 ballot, they can pursue the initial signature threshold next fall, when the requirement will be based on votes cast in this month's gubernatorial election.","That approach gives organizers more time to build public support and leaves them an opportunity to submit alternative versions of the proposal by next August's filing deadline. Fleming indicated the language already approved by the attorney general may not be the version ultimately advanced.","Filing early also puts lawmakers on notice as they begin a legislative session in January. If enough signatures are collected next fall, the Legislature would have until early May 2028 to act on the proposal. If lawmakers do not pass it, supporters would need to gather a smaller round of signatures by early July to secure a spot on the November ballot.","Fleming said the prospect of a ballot question is intended, in part, to prompt legislative action before voters are asked to decide the issue.","\"If the legislature passes a law like this that is good, and not just an executive order, then we will wrap this entire process. And this will hopefully encourage them to do this,\" he said.","The petition would go further than \u003ca href=\"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/08/proposed-data-centers-local-approvals-healey-massachusetts\"\u003eGov. Maura Healey's executive order\u003c/a\u003e, signed Sept. 8, which established requirements for state agencies reviewing large data center projects. The order generally applies to facilities exceeding 25 megawatts, while the petition sets a lower threshold of 5 megawatts of peak annual demand.","Healey's order directs state agencies, including the Department of Environmental Protection and the Energy Facilities Siting Board, to develop policies addressing electricity, water, environmental impacts and community benefits. It requires developers to procure incremental clean electricity, with an alternative compliance payment available, and directs agencies to develop ratepayer protections.","Unlike the proposed ballot measure, the order does not require a community-wide vote. Instead, it calls for community benefit agreements and municipal guidance. It also applies only to facilities built or expanded after it took effect.","Like any executive order, it can be amended or revoked by a future governor.","The campaign is emerging amid broader political resistance to data centers. Voters favored restrictions in 40 of 41 local ballot contests held this past Election Day, with measures passing in Ohio, California, Florida, Kansas, Maine, Illinois and Wisconsin, according to Ballotopedia.","In Ohio, the advocacy group Conserve Ohio filed a proposed measure in March that would prohibit data centers statewide with aggregate power demands exceeding 25 megawatts. It's targeting the 2027 ballot for a vote.","Although the petition would not prohibit data centers outright, its combination of energy and financial requirements, and a two-thirds local vote could make approval substantially more difficult and may discourage interested developers."],"enhanced":false,"seriesMeta":null,"iframeHero":null,"postType":"post","isBreaking":false,"isDeveloping":false,"relatedLinks":[{"url":"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/22/new-england-ai-data-centers-explainer","title":"Why New England doesn't have large AI data centers, and what the region is doing to prepare for them","prefix":""},{"url":"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/23/new-england-data-centers-retrofitting","title":"New England’s old buildings and old data centers could be upgraded to handle AI computing","prefix":""},{"url":"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/07/29/lowell-data-center-massachusetts-markley-group-environmental-justice","title":"Residents want a judge to pause Lowell data center expansion","prefix":""},{"url":"https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/08/proposed-data-centers-local-approvals-healey-massachusetts","title":"Proposed data centers subjected to local approvals under Gov.
